funFacts.text: Aruba's divi-divi trees act as natural compasses: shaped by the constant trade winds, they always point southwest.
Aruba lies south of the main hurricane breeding zone and generally avoids direct hits from hurricanes.
Aruba's California Lighthouse is named after the British steamship California, which sank just offshore in 1891.
Arikok National Park protects about a fifth of Aruba, including limestone caves with ancient Arawak paintings.
A 12-year-old herder found gold on Aruba in 1824, sparking the Aruban Gold Rush.
The Aruban burrowing owl, called the 'shoco', became the island's official national symbol in 2015.
The intensely blue Band-e Amir lakes are held back by natural travertine walls and became Afghanistan's first national park in 2009.
The Sar-i Sang mines in Badakhshan have been dug for blue lapis lazuli for more than 6,000 years.
Buzkashi, in which riders on horseback try to get a goat or calf carcass into a goal, is Afghanistan's national sport.
The elegant, long-haired Afghan hound comes from the cold mountains of Afghanistan, where it was bred for speed.
Afghanistan's national dish, Kabuli pulao, is rice cooked with raisins, carrots, nuts and lamb or beef.
The 65-metre Minaret of Jam, built around 1190 in a remote region, became Afghanistan's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2002.
The giant sable antelope, with huge sweeping horns, lives only in Angola and has been a national emblem since 1975.
Kalandula Falls on the Lucala River, 105 m high and 400 m wide, is one of the largest waterfalls by volume in Africa.
Welwitschia, a strange desert plant that only ever grows two leaves, lives in the Namib Desert of Angola and Namibia.
Kizomba, a slow and smooth partner dance now popular worldwide, originated in Angola around the late 1970s and early 1980s.
The Cubango River rises in Angola's highlands and flows on as the Okavango into Botswana's famous Okavango Delta.
Angola's province of Cabinda is an exclave, separated from the rest of the country by a narrow strip of DR Congo.
Anguilla's internet domain is .ai, and in 2023 the AI boom earned its government about US$32 million in web address fees.
Anguilla's name comes from the Italian word for 'eel', inspired by the island's long, narrow shape.
Boat racing is Anguilla's national sport and has deep roots in the island's culture.
Anguilla's Sombrero island got its name because from the sea it looked like a sombrero hat, and its lighthouse guides passing ships.
Anguilla's Fountain Cavern holds as many as 33 ancient Amerindian rock carvings, one thought to show the god Jocahu.
Anguilla is a flat, low-lying island made of coral and limestone.
In parts of southern Albania, nodding your head can mean 'no' and shaking it can mean 'yes'.
Butrint, an ancient Greek city that later became Roman, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site in southern Albania.
Berat is nicknamed the 'Town of One Window Above the Other' for the many large windows of its old houses on the hillside.
Lake Ohrid, which Albania shares with North Macedonia, is one of Europe's deepest and oldest lakes.
The Albanian language forms its own separate branch of the Indo-European language family.
Albanian folk iso-polyphony, a style of multi-voice singing, has been on UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage list since 2008.
Åland is made up of about 6,500 islands and skerries, and Swedish is its sole official language even though it belongs to Finland.
Åland has issued its own postage stamps since 1 March 1984.
The four-masted barque Pommern is now a museum ship anchored in Mariehamn, Åland's capital.
Åland pancake is an oven-baked treat made with semolina or rice, served with prune jam and whipped cream.
Åland has its own internet domain, .ax.
Åland's flag looks like Sweden's flag with an extra red cross added to symbolise Finland.
Andorra has two heads of state at the same time: the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell in Spain.
Andorra la Vella, at 1,023 metres above sea level, is the highest capital city in Europe.
Andorra has never had a railway, and there's no airport for planes inside its borders.
Catalan is the sole official language of Andorra.
The Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley, a glacial valley with old stone shepherd huts, is Andorra's only UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Andorra's Grandvalira is the largest ski area in the Pyrenees, with about 205 km of ski runs.
Dubai's Burj Khalifa, at 828 metres, is the tallest building in the world.
Palm Jumeirah in Dubai is a group of artificial islands built to look like a palm tree from the air.
Ski Dubai is an indoor ski resort with an 85-metre-high snowy mountain inside the Mall of the Emirates, in the middle of the desert.
Falcons are so treasured in the UAE that more than 28,000 of them have been issued their own passports.
In UAE camel racing, remote-controlled robot jockeys ride the camels instead of people.
Formula Rossa at Ferrari World Abu Dhabi reaches 240 km/h and was the world's fastest roller coaster when it opened.
Aconcagua, at nearly 7,000 metres, is the highest mountain anywhere outside Asia.
Iguazú Falls, on Argentina's border with Brazil, is split into roughly 275 separate falls.
Perito Moreno Glacier sometimes dams part of Lake Argentino until the water pressure bursts spectacularly through the ice.
The tango was born in the working-class districts of Buenos Aires and Montevideo in the 1880s.
Ushuaia, on Tierra del Fuego, has long been described as the southernmost city in the world.
Argentinosaurus, one of the largest land animals of all time, was found in Argentina, and its name means 'Argentine lizard'.
The world's oldest known leather shoe, about 5,500 years old, was found in Armenia's Areni-1 cave.
The Areni-1 cave also holds the world's oldest known winery, over 6,000 years old.
Armenian lavash, a thin bread slapped against the walls of a clay oven, joined UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2014.
The 5.7 km Wings of Tatev cable car holds the record for the longest non-stop double-track cable car.
In 2011 Armenia became the first country in the world to make chess a compulsory school subject.
The Armenian alphabet was created around 405 AD by the scholar Mesrop Mashtots.

ASM.capitalNote: The government offices are in Fagatogo, a village within the Pago Pago harbour area.

funFacts.text: The National Park of American Samoa is the only US national park south of the equator.
Pago Pago Harbor is what's left of an old volcanic crater and is one of the deepest harbours in the South Pacific.
Tiny Rose Atoll in American Samoa is the southernmost point of the United States.
Per person, the Samoan Islands have produced more NFL football players than anywhere else.
The National Park of American Samoa was created partly to protect the habitat of the flying fox, a large fruit bat.
About 70% of the world's fresh water is frozen in Antarctica's ice.
The lowest natural temperature ever recorded, -89.2°C, was measured at Russia's Vostok Station in Antarctica in 1983.
Because it gets so little precipitation, Antarctica is the world's largest cold desert.
Male emperor penguins balance their egg on top of their feet for over two months to keep it warm.
Blood Falls is a glacier outflow that stains the ice red with iron-rich salty water flowing from Taylor Glacier.
Mount Erebus, the southernmost active volcano on Earth, has a long-lived lake of lava in its crater.
Ashmore Reef is a protected marine park and a stopover for about 30 species of migrating shorebirds.
The Ashmore and Cartier Islands are uninhabited, with no permanent residents at all.
Ashmore Reef is named after Captain Samuel Ashmore, who sighted it from the ship Hibernia in 1811.
Ashmore Reef was once known as a global hotspot for sea snakes.
Ashmore Reef Marine Park is Ramsar-listed, and green, hawksbill and loggerhead turtles breed and feed there.

ATF.capitalNote: The main base, on the Kerguelen Islands. The territory is administered from Saint-Pierre on Réunion.

funFacts.text: Captain James Cook named the windswept Kerguelen Islands the 'Desolation Islands' because the landscape looked so barren.
The vitamin-rich Kerguelen cabbage was a welcome food for old-time sailors suffering from scurvy.
Adélie Land was named by explorer Dumont d'Urville after his wife Adèle, and the Adélie penguin is named after it.
The Crozet Islands host about 700,000 breeding pairs of king penguins, half the world's population.
The French Southern and Antarctic Lands have no permanent population, only visiting scientists, officials and staff.
The endangered Amsterdam albatross breeds in only one place on Earth: Amsterdam Island.
Antigua and Barbuda are said to have 365 beaches, one for every day of the year.
Nelson's Dockyard in English Harbour is the only continuously working Georgian-era dockyard in the world.
Barbuda's Codrington Lagoon is home to the largest magnificent frigatebird colony in the world.
Antigua Sailing Week, founded in 1967, is one of the top sailing regattas in the world.
Barbuda is famous for its pink beaches, coloured by the tiniest of pink shells washed ashore.
A pineapple, a fruit the islands are famous for, sits at the very top of Antigua and Barbuda's coat of arms.
Australia's wombats are famous for producing cube-shaped poo.
The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system and can be seen from outer space.
Platypuses and echidnas, the only mammals that lay eggs, are native to Australia and New Guinea.
Australia's Dingo Fence, 5,614 km long, is one of the longest structures in the world.
The flight data recorder or 'black box' was invented by Australian scientist David Warren.
Uluru, a giant sandstone monolith in the Outback, seems to change colour and glows red at dawn and sunset.
Vienna's Schönbrunn Zoo, founded in 1752, is the oldest zoo in the world that is still operating.
Eisriesenwelt near Werfen is the largest ice cave in the world, stretching more than 42 km into the mountain.
The famous chocolate Sachertorte was invented by Franz Sacher in the 19th century.
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, and his birthplace has been a museum since 1880.
The Riesenrad Ferris wheel in Vienna's Prater park has been turning since 1897.
Erwin Perzy helped make the snow globe famous, and his family still makes them in Vienna today.
Baku lies 28 metres below sea level, making it the lowest-lying national capital in the world.
Yanar Dag is a hillside near Baku where natural gas seeping from the ground keeps a fire burning all the time.
Azerbaijan and its Caspian coast have nearly 400 mud volcanoes, more than half of all those on the continents.
Gobustan has over 6,000 ancient rock carvings and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007.
Azerbaijani mugham, a traditional music full of improvisation, is on UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage list.
The world's first drilled oil well was sunk at Bibi-Heybat near Baku in 1846.

BDI.capitalNote: Gitega became the political capital in 2019; Bujumbura remains the largest city and economic capital.

funFacts.text: The southernmost source of the Nile is in Burundi, marked by a monument near the town of Rutovu.
Lake Tanganyika, on Burundi's border, is the second-deepest lake in the world.
Burundi's Ritual Dance of the Royal Drum, with synchronised drumming and dancing, joined UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2014.
Kibira National Park protects Burundi's only mountain rainforest, home to chimpanzees.
Coffee and tea are Burundi's main exports, bringing in 90% of its foreign earnings.
Lake Tanganyika is home to at least 250 kinds of cichlid fish found nowhere else.
The saxophone was invented by Belgian instrument maker Adolphe Sax in the early 1840s.
Brussels' Atomium, built for the 1958 World's Fair, represents an iron crystal magnified 165 billion times.
The Smurfs were created by the Belgian comic artist Peyo.
Belgian beer culture was added to UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage in 2016.
Belgian priest and physicist Georges Lemaître came up with the first version of the Big Bang theory.
Brussels' tiny Manneken Pis statue has a wardrobe of around 1,000 costumes.

BEN.capitalNote: Porto-Novo is the official capital, while Cotonou is the seat of government and largest city.

funFacts.text: Ganvié, a lake village on Lake Nokoué with around 20,000 people, is often called the 'Venice of Africa'.
The Royal Palaces of Abomey, home of the kings of Dahomey, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985.
The W-Arly-Pendjari park complex, shared with Burkina Faso and Niger, holds the largest concentration of elephants in West Africa.
In Koutammakou, the Batammariba people still live in traditional mud tower-houses.
Benin was called Dahomey until 1975, when it was renamed after the Bight of Benin.
Cotton makes up roughly 80% of Benin's official export earnings.
Ouagadougou hosts FESPACO, the main event of African cinema, held every two years since it was founded in 1969.
The name Burkina Faso, built from Mooré and Dyula words, means 'land of honest men' (literally 'land of the upright men').
In Tiébélé, the earthen walls of Kassena houses are painted with geometric shapes and symbols of local folklore.
The Ruins of Loropéni, stone walls at least 1,000 years old, became Burkina Faso's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2009.
Every two years Ouagadougou hosts SIAO, one of Africa's most important arts and crafts trade shows.
Burkina Faso shares the W-Arly-Pendjari complex, a UNESCO site, with Benin and Niger, and it is a stronghold for lions.
The Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest, is home to Bengal tigers that swim between its mangrove islands.
Cox's Bazar Beach runs for 120 km and is the longest natural sea beach in Asia.
Bangladesh sits on the fertile Ganges Delta, the largest river delta in the world.
In 2023 UNESCO added Dhaka's rickshaws and colourful rickshaw paintings to its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.
The ilish (hilsa) is Bangladesh's national fish, and shorshe ilish, cooked with mustard seeds, is a Bengali classic.
Somapura Mahavihara at Paharpur, a UNESCO site since 1985, was the largest of the great ancient Buddhist monasteries by area.
Bulgaria's Rose Valley produces close to half of all the world's rose oil.
The early Cyrillic alphabet was developed in the 9th century at the Preslav Literary School in the First Bulgarian Empire.
In Bulgaria, a single upward nod of the head means 'no', so watch your head when you answer!
The yogurt bacterium Lactobacillus bulgaricus was first identified in 1905 by Bulgarian doctor Stamen Grigorov.
From 1 March, Bulgarians wear red-and-white martenitsa threads, given as gifts to herald the coming of spring.
The Varna Necropolis held the oldest gold treasure in the world, dating from 4600 to 4200 BC.
Bahrain's 'Tree of Life' is a lone mesquite over 400 years old in the desert, and no one is sure how it survives.
Bahrain is an archipelago of 33 natural islands plus about 50 artificial ones.
Bahrain's Dilmun Burial Mounds, left by the Bronze Age Dilmun culture, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019.
Bahrain's Pearling Path in Muharraq became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012, honouring its pearl-diving past.
In 2004, Bahrain hosted the first Formula One Grand Prix ever held in the Middle East.
The King Fahd Causeway, a 25 km chain of bridges and causeways, links Bahrain to Saudi Arabia.
Big Major Cay in the Exumas is home to a colony of wild pigs famous as the Bahamas' swimming pigs.
Dean's Blue Hole on Long Island plunges 202 m deep and hosts the Vertical Blue freediving competition.
Christopher Columbus made his first landfall in the New World in 1492 on San Salvador in the Bahamas.
Inagua National Park has the world's largest breeding colony of West Indian flamingos, over 50,000 birds.
Junkanoo is a dazzling Bahamian parade of intricate costumes, goatskin drums and cowbells on Boxing Day and New Year's Day.
From 1713 to 1718 pirates ran Nassau as their own 'Republic of Pirates', with Blackbeard among them.
Young men of Mostar traditionally leap from the 24-metre-high Old Bridge into the cold Neretva River.
Sarajevo hosted the 1984 Winter Olympics, the first held in a Slavic-speaking country.
Perućica in Sutjeska National Park is one of the last remaining primeval forests in Europe.
Višegrad's Mehmed Paša Sokolović Bridge, a UNESCO site since 2007, stars in Nobel winner Ivo Andrić's 'The Bridge on the Drina'.
At Jajce, the Pliva River tumbles 22 metres down a waterfall to meet the Vrbas.
Ćevapi, grilled minced-meat sausages served in somun flatbread, are considered a national dish of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Bajo Nuevo Bank is also known as the Petrel Islands.
Bajo Nuevo is an uninhabited reef in the western Caribbean Sea with a few small grass-covered islets.
Its main islet, Low Cay, is made of nothing but broken coral, driftwood and sand.
A 21-metre metal light beacon stands on Low Cay, looked after by the Colombian Navy.
Gustavia is named after Swedish King Gustav III, because Sweden ruled the island for nearly a century.
Planes landing at St Barth's very short airstrip make an extremely steep descent over a hilltop traffic circle.
Columbus named the island after Saint Bartholomew, which also honoured his younger brother Bartholomew.
Saint Barthélemy is still a free port, and its economy runs on tourism and duty-free shopping.
Each April, racing yachts gather in Gustavia for the Les Voiles de St. Barth regatta.
Białowieża Forest, straddling the Belarus–Poland border, is home to more than 800 European bison, Europe's heaviest land animal.
Lake Narach is the largest lake in Belarus and a popular holiday resort.
Belarus's fairy-tale Mir Castle was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.
Draniki, Belarusian potato pancakes, are a national dish of Belarus.
The Pripet Marshes of Polesia, mostly in Belarus, are the largest wetland area in Europe.
Painter Marc Chagall was born in 1887 near Vitebsk, and his childhood home there is now the Marc Chagall Museum.
The Great Blue Hole is a giant circular underwater sinkhole 318 m across and 124 m deep.
The Belize Barrier Reef is part of the second-largest coral reef system in the world, after the Great Barrier Reef.
Cockscomb Basin, set up in 1986, was the first protected area created especially for jaguars.
Belize is the only country in Central America where English is the official language.
Caracol was one of the largest ancient Maya cities, and its 43 m Caana is the tallest man-made structure in Belize.
The colourful keel-billed toucan is the national bird of Belize.
Bermuda's beaches get their pink tint from Homotrema rubrum, a bright red foraminifer ground into sand by the surf.
In Bermuda, Bermuda shorts in suit-like fabric, worn with knee socks and a blazer, are proper business attire.
Bermuda's only source of fresh water is rain, which is collected on roofs and stored in tanks.
The 1609 wreck of the Sea Venture on Bermuda is believed to have inspired Shakespeare's 'The Tempest'.
The cahow, Bermuda's national bird, was thought extinct for 300 years until 18 nesting pairs were found in 1951.
Warmed by the Gulf Stream, Bermuda's coral reefs are the northernmost in the Atlantic Ocean.

BOL.capitalNote: Sucre is the constitutional capital, while La Paz is the seat of government.

funFacts.text: Salar de Uyuni is the world's largest salt flat, and after rain it turns into the world's largest mirror.
Mi Teleférico, the cable car linking La Paz and El Alto, is the longest aerial cable car system in the world.
Lake Titicaca, on the Bolivia–Peru border at 3,812 m, is often called the highest navigable lake in the world.
Potosí's Cerro Rico, Spanish for 'Rich Mountain', supplied vast quantities of silver to the Spanish Empire.
Near Sucre, the Cal Orck'o cliff holds 12,092 dinosaur tracks in 465 trackways.
In 2018 Madidi was named the world's most biologically diverse national park.
Brazil is the most successful team in World Cup history, with five titles, and has played in every edition.
About 58% of the Amazon rainforest lies within Brazil's borders.
Rio de Janeiro's Carnival is considered the biggest Carnival celebration in the world.
The Pantanal is the world's largest tropical wetland and home to one of Earth's healthiest jaguar populations.
Brazil has been the world's largest coffee producer for the last 150 years.
In Lençóis Maranhenses, rainy-season water fills freshwater lagoons between sand dunes up to 40 m tall.
The grapefruit originated in Barbados in the 18th century as an accidental cross of sweet orange and pomelo.
Mount Gay, whose oldest surviving deed dates from 1703, is called the world's oldest commercial rum distillery.
Barbados is the only place outside the United States that George Washington ever visited, in 1751.
Crop Over, Barbados's end-of-harvest festival, began on the sugar cane plantations, with roots going back to 1687.
Cou-cou, made from cornmeal and okra, with flying fish is the national dish of Barbados.
Visitors explore Harrison's Cave by tram, past stalactites and stalagmites formed in the limestone.
Kampong Ayer is a village built on stilts above the Brunei River, nicknamed the 'Venice of the East'.
Guinness World Records ranks the Sultan's Istana Nurul Iman, with 1,788 rooms, as the world's largest residential palace.
Ulu Temburong, the 'Green Jewel of Brunei', has a canopy walkway 50 metres above the rainforest floor.
Brunei is split into two separate parts by Limbang, a district of the Malaysian state of Sarawak.
Ambuyat, Brunei's national dish, is sticky sago starch eaten with linked bamboo chopsticks called chandas.
Big-nosed proboscis monkeys live mostly in mangrove forests on Borneo, including in Brunei.
Bir Tawil is the only habitable place on Earth not claimed by any recognised government.
Bir Tawil means 'tall water well' in Arabic.
Egypt and Sudan follow different border lines, so both claim the Halaib Triangle and neither wants Bir Tawil.
Many people have tried to claim Bir Tawil as their own micronation, but no government has recognised any of them.
Thimphu is one of only two national capitals without traffic lights; traffic police direct the cars instead.
Bhutan measures its people's happiness and well-being with a Gross National Happiness Index.
Bhutan is carbon-neutral and even a net sink for greenhouse gases, absorbing more than it emits.
Archery is Bhutan's national sport, and fans try to distract opponents with funny gestures and humorous insults.
Bhutan's Gangkhar Puensum (7,570 m) is the highest unclimbed mountain in the world.
The takin, a stocky goat relative from the eastern Himalayas, is Bhutan's national animal.
Bouvet Island has been called the most remote island in the world; the nearest land, Antarctica, is about 1,700 km away.
About 93% of Bouvet Island is covered by glaciers, giving it a domed shape.
Explorer Jean-Baptiste Bouvet spotted the island through fog in 1739 while searching for a supposed southern continent.
In 1964 a survey team landing on Bouvet Island found a mysterious abandoned lifeboat in a small lagoon.
Bouvet Island has its own internet domain, .bv, but it is not in use.
Since 1971 the whole island has been a nature reserve, where thousands of fur seals and penguins breed.
The Okavango Delta never reaches the sea; nearly all its water evaporates in the Kalahari basin.
In 2014 the Okavango Delta became the 1,000th site inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List.
Botswana has more African bush elephants than any other country, about 130,000.
The Makgadikgadi Pan, one of the world's largest salt flats, hosts one of southern Africa's only two breeding groups of greater flamingos.
The Tsodilo Hills, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, hold over 4,500 rock paintings.
Botswana's currency, the pula, means 'rain' in Setswana, because rain is so scarce there.
At Dzanga Bai, large numbers of forest elephants gather to feed on mineral-rich soils.
At Bai Hokou in Dzanga-Sangha, visitors can track western lowland gorillas used to people, guided by Aka trackers.
The Central African Republic is named for its location in Central Africa and its republican government.
The Boali Falls, 250 m wide and 50 m high, are a popular sight about 100 km from Bangui.
The Aka people's four-voice polyphonic singing was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2008.
Manovo-Gounda St Floris National Park, a UNESCO site since 1988, is home to elephants, cheetahs, leopards and lions.
Canada has the longest coastline in the world, a whopping 243,042 km.
Canada has over 2 million lakes, more than any other country.
The Bay of Fundy has the highest tidal range in the world, about 16 metres.
Quebec alone produces about 72% of the world's maple syrup.
Banting and Best first isolated insulin at the University of Toronto in 1921.
The world's largest beaver dam, about 850 m long, was spotted in Wood Buffalo National Park using satellite images.
Charles Darwin visited aboard HMS Beagle in 1836, and what he saw supported his theory of how coral atolls form.
Only two of the 27 coral islands are inhabited: West Island and Home Island.
For almost 150 years the Clunies-Ross family ruled the islands as their own private fiefdom.
North Keeling Island may have the largest red-footed booby colony in the world.
In 2016 a beach on Direction Island was named the best beach in Australia.
The name 'Cocos' comes from the islands' many coconut trees.

CHE.capitalNote: Switzerland has no official capital; Bern is the 'federal city' and seat of government.

funFacts.text: The Gotthard Base Tunnel, about 57 km long, is the longest railway tunnel in the world.
Switzerland's flag is square, and the only other square national flag is Vatican City's.
Swiss chocolatier Daniel Peter invented milk chocolate in the 1870s, with help from his Vevey neighbour Henri Nestlé.
Swiss engineer George de Mestral invented Velcro after noticing how burdock burrs stuck to his dog's fur.
The World Wide Web was invented in 1989 by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in Geneva.
Jungfraujoch station, at 3,454 metres, is the highest railway station in Europe.
The Atacama Desert is the driest non-polar desert on Earth; some weather stations there have never recorded rain.
Chile stretches about 4,270 km from north to south but averages only 177 km wide.
Easter Island, home to nearly 1,000 giant moai statues, is part of Chile.
Castaway Alexander Selkirk, who helped inspire Robinson Crusoe, lived on a Chilean island that was renamed Robinson Crusoe Island in 1966.
Chile has been the world's largest producer of copper every year since 1983.
The ALMA radio telescope sits on Chile's Chajnantor plateau, 5,000 metres up in the dry Atacama.
Although China spans five geographical time zones, the whole country runs on a single official time.
Including all its branches, the Great Wall of China stretches more than 21,000 km.
The compass, gunpowder, papermaking and printing are celebrated as ancient China's Four Great Inventions.
Wild giant pandas live only in China, mostly in the mountains of Sichuan.
The Terracotta Army of more than 8,000 clay soldiers was buried with China's first emperor, Qin Shi Huang.
The Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze River is the world's largest power station by installed capacity.

CIV.capitalNote: Yamoussoukro is the official capital, while Abidjan is the economic capital and hosts most government offices.

funFacts.text: Côte d'Ivoire is the world's largest cocoa producer, growing about 45% of the world's cocoa.
The country's name comes from the ivory trade that European traders carried on along its coast.
Guinness World Records lists Yamoussoukro's Basilica of Our Lady of Peace, inspired by St Peter's in Rome, as the largest church in the world.
Chimpanzees in Côte d'Ivoire's Taï forest use stone and wooden hammers to crack open nuts.
Attiéké, made from fermented cassava with a texture like couscous, is a popular traditional Ivorian dish.
Côte d'Ivoire won the 2023 Africa Cup of Nations on home soil.
The atoll's lagoon was sealed off from the sea about 170 years ago, and bright-orange Clipperton crabs roam the land.
The island is named after John Clipperton, an English pirate and privateer said to have passed by it.
Clipperton Rock, a volcanic outcrop about 29 metres tall, is the highest point on the otherwise flat atoll.
Clipperton has the world's largest colony of masked boobies.
After pigs were removed in 1958, the island's masked boobies grew from about 150 birds to over 100,000.
Cameroon is nicknamed 'Africa in miniature' because it has all the continent's major climates, from coast and rainforest to desert and mountains.
Mount Cameroon, an active volcano about 4,040 metres tall, is the highest point in sub-Saharan western and central Africa.
Debundscha, at the foot of Mount Cameroon, is one of the five rainiest places in the world, with over 10 metres of rain a year.
The goliath frog, the largest frog in the world, lives only in Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea.
In 1990 Cameroon became the first African team to reach the quarter-finals of the FIFA World Cup.
Cameroonians speak about 250 native languages, and both French and English are official languages.
The Congo River is the deepest recorded river in the world, with depths of around 220 metres.
The okapi, a giraffe relative with zebra-like stripes, lives in the wild only in the DR Congo.
Bonobos, which share the title of humans' closest living relative with chimpanzees, live in the Congo Basin forests of the DR Congo.
Virunga National Park, founded in 1925, is Africa's oldest national park and a home of mountain gorillas.
Mount Nyiragongo's lava lake has at times been the largest known lava lake on Earth by volume.
The Congo is the only major river to cross the equator twice.
Brazzaville and Kinshasa are the only two national capitals that face each other across a river, within sight of each other.
Brazzaville is named after the explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza.
Odzala-Kokoua, first protected in 1935, is one of Africa's oldest national parks and a home of western lowland gorillas.
The 'sapeurs' of the Congo are famous for their love of luxury fashion and designer brands.
Congolese rumba, shared with the DR Congo, was added to UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage in 2021.
Nouabalé-Ndoki National Park is part of the Sangha Trinational, a UNESCO World Heritage forest shared with Cameroon and the Central African Republic.
The Cook Islands still use a $3 banknote, and in 1987 became the first modern country to issue a triangular coin.
The islands are named after Captain James Cook, who visited them in 1773 and 1777.
Marae Moana, created in 2017, protects the islands' entire ocean area of over 1.9 million square kilometres.
Rarotonga's two bus routes are simply called 'clockwise' and 'anticlockwise' around the island.
Tapuaetai, or One Foot Island, is said to have the best views of Aitutaki's turquoise lagoon.
Colombia has more bird species than any other country, with over 1,900 recorded.
Caño Cristales is called the 'River of Five Colors' because a water plant turns its bed bright red.
Colombia produces more emeralds than any other country.
Colombia is one of only two South American countries with coastlines on both the Atlantic and the Pacific.
The Quindío wax palm, Colombia's national tree, is the tallest recorded monocot, rarely reaching 60 metres.
Colombian writer Gabriel García Márquez won the 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature and wrote 'One Hundred Years of Solitude'.
The coelacanth, a 'living fossil' fish known only from fossils until 1938, lives on the undersea slopes around the Comoros.
Once called the 'Perfume Islands', the Comoros are the world's largest producer of ylang-ylang, used in perfumes.
Mount Karthala on Grande Comore is a very active volcano that has erupted more than 20 times since the 1800s.
Livingstone's fruit bat, the largest bat in the Comoros, lives only on the islands of Anjouan and Mohéli.
The name Comoros comes from Arabic words meaning 'Islands of the Moon'.
On Grande Comore, a lavish 'grand marriage' can last two weeks and cost up to €50,000.
About 700 people live inside the crater of Fogo's volcano, where all the grapes for the island's wine are grown.
Singer Cesária Évora, the 'Barefoot Diva', was the world's best-known performer of Cape Verde's morna music.
The islands were uninhabited when Europeans discovered them around 1456.
Cape Verde is the only significant nesting site for loggerhead sea turtles on the eastern side of the Atlantic.
Cachupa, a slow-cooked stew of corn, beans and fish or meat, is the national dish.
On Sal island, the salt pans of Pedra de Lume lie inside the crater of an extinct volcano.
Costa Rica covers just 1/30 of a percent of Earth's land but is home to nearly 5% of all known species.
'Pura vida', meaning 'pure life', is one of Costa Rica's most recognisable phrases.
Over 300 ancient stone spheres, some almost perfectly round, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014.
Over 27% of Costa Rica's land is protected.
Tortuguero, meaning 'Land of Turtles', has key nesting beaches for four species of sea turtle.
In 2019 Costa Rica produced 99.62% of its electricity from renewable sources.
A weather station on Willis Island has provided cyclone warnings for Queensland since 1921.
Willis Island is the only permanently inhabited island in the territory, usually home to four weather observers.
The territory's small islands and reefs are spread over 780,000 km² of sea but add up to only about 7 km² of land.
The surrounding Coral Sea Marine Park, almost 990,000 km², is Australia's largest single marine park.
The bee hummingbird, the smallest bird in the world, lives only in Cuba.
An estimated 60,000 classic American cars, nicknamed 'yank tanks', are still driving on Cuba's roads.
The daiquiri cocktail was invented in Cuba and named after a beach near Santiago de Cuba.
The Cuban solenodon is one of the few venomous mammals and was once thought extinct until it was rediscovered in 1974.
Cuban chess genius José Raúl Capablanca was world chess champion from 1921 to 1927.
The Viñales Valley, a UNESCO site, is famous for tobacco farms among limestone hills called mogotes.
Willemstad's Queen Emma Bridge is a floating pontoon bridge that swings open to let ocean-going ships pass.
Blue Curaçao liqueur is flavoured with the dried peel of the laraha, a bitter orange grown on the island.
Willemstad's historic centre, with its unique architecture and harbour entrance, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997.
The sand-floored Mikvé Israel-Emanuel Synagogue is the oldest surviving synagogue in the Americas.
Papiamentu, the local language, is largely based on Portuguese, with many Spanish, Dutch and African words.
Every year the island's red crabs march to the sea to lay their eggs, and roads are closed to let them pass.
The island got its name because Captain William Mynors sailed past it on Christmas Day in 1643.
Christmas Island has the world's largest population of robber crabs, the largest land-living invertebrates on Earth.
Abbott's booby, a rare seabird, nests only in the tall rainforest of Christmas Island.
About 63% of the island is protected as Christmas Island National Park.
Phosphate has been mined on the island since 1899.
Grand Cayman has an area called Hell, where visitors can mail 'postcards from hell' from a bright red post office.
At Stingray City, visitors stand in just 3 feet of water on a sandbar while southern stingrays glide around them.
The blue iguana lives only on Grand Cayman; fewer than 15 were left in the wild in 2003, but about 750 by 2012.
Christopher Columbus called the islands 'Las Tortugas' in 1503 because of the many sea turtles there.
The name 'Cayman' comes from a Carib word for the crocodile-like reptiles that once lived on the islands.
Little Cayman's Bloody Bay Wall is a famous dive site where a reef wall drops more than 300 metres.
According to legend, the goddess Aphrodite was born from the sea foam at Petra tou Romiou on Cyprus's south coast.
Halloumi, the squeaky cheese that's perfect for grilling, comes from Cyprus.
The English word 'copper' comes from the Latin 'aes cyprium', meaning 'metal of Cyprus'.
Commandaria, a sweet dessert wine, is considered the oldest named wine still in production.
A cat buried with a person about 9,500 years ago at Shillourokambos is the oldest evidence of humans taming cats.
The Cyprus mouflon, a shy wild sheep with curved horns, is the island's national animal.
Czechs drink more beer per person than people in any other country, about 126 litres a year.
The oldest parts of Prague's famous astronomical clock, the Orloj, date back to 1410.
The first sugar cubes were made in Dačice in the early 1840s by Jakub Kryštof Rad, who patented them in 1843.
The word 'robot' comes from Karel Čapek's 1920 Czech play R.U.R.
According to Guinness World Records, Prague Castle is the largest ancient castle in the world.
Czech chemist Otto Wichterle invented soft contact lenses, building an early machine with a children's construction kit.
German bread culture is on Germany's national list of intangible cultural heritage, and the country bakes more than 3,000 types of bread.
Johannes Gutenberg invented the movable-type printing press around 1440, and his print shop in Mainz was at first the only one in Europe.
More than half of Germany's Autobahn network has no speed limit, just an advisory speed of 130 km/h.
Bavaria's fairytale Neuschwanstein Castle inspired Disneyland's Sleeping Beauty Castle.
The first Oktoberfest was held in 1810 to celebrate the wedding of Crown Prince Ludwig and Princess Therese.
In 1922 Haribo founder Hans Riegel, a confectioner from Bonn, invented the 'Dancing Bear', the ancestor of today's gummy bears.
Djibouti's Lake Assal lies 155 metres below sea level, the lowest point on land in Africa, and is one of the saltiest lakes on Earth.
Djibouti's Lake Abbe is famous for limestone chimneys up to 50 metres tall that spew out steam.
Between November and February, young whale sharks gather to feed in the plankton-rich Gulf of Tadjoura off Djibouti.
Djibouti sits on the Bab-el-Mandeb, the 'Gate of Grief' strait linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Djibouti's Lake Assal lies in the Afar Triangle, where three major tectonic plates are moving apart and stretching the land.
The Djiboutian franc has been pegged to the US dollar since 1949.
Dominica's Boiling Lake is a flooded volcanic vent full of bubbling grey-blue water, the second-largest hot lake in the world.
Dominica's flag shows the Sisserou parrot, making it one of the few national flags with the colour purple.
Morne Trois Pitons National Park, with volcanoes, hot springs and rainforest, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997.
Scenes from Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Man's Chest were filmed on Dominica in 2005.
The Kalinago Territory on Dominica's east coast is the largest settlement of Indigenous people in the Caribbean.
A group of sperm whales lives off Dominica all year round, making it a top whale-watching spot.
LEGO began in a carpenter's workshop in Billund, Denmark; its name comes from the Danish 'leg godt', meaning 'play well'.
Denmark's flag, the Dannebrog, holds the Guinness world record as the oldest continuously used national flag.
Bakken, north of Copenhagen, opened in 1583 and is the world's oldest operating amusement park.
Copenhagen's Little Mermaid statue, unveiled in 1913, is based on the fairy tale by Danish author Hans Christian Andersen.
Denmark's Vindeby, which started operating in 1991, was the world's first offshore wind farm.
In Denmark, Danish pastries are called 'wienerbrød', meaning 'Viennese bread'.
Larimar, a blue gemstone, is found only in the Dominican Republic, around the city of Barahona.
Santo Domingo, founded in 1496, is the oldest continuously inhabited European settlement in the Americas.
Pico Duarte, at 3,101 metres, is the highest mountain in the whole Caribbean.
Lake Enriquillo, the largest lake in the Caribbean, lies 46 metres below sea level and is home to American crocodiles and rhinoceros iguanas.
Merengue, the national music and dance of the Dominican Republic, joined UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2016.
Samaná Bay is one of the Caribbean's key breeding sites for humpback whales, drawing many whale-watchers.
Algeria is Africa's largest country, and the Sahara covers most of it except the fertile, mountainous north.
About 15,000 prehistoric engravings have been found at Tassili n'Ajjer, showing wild animals, cattle herds and people hunting and dancing.
The M'zab Valley's five fortified towns were founded between 1012 and 1350 and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982.
Timgad, founded by Emperor Trajan in 100 AD, still shows its original Roman grid of streets.
Couscous joined UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2020, a joint bid by Algeria, Mauritania, Morocco and Tunisia.
Raï music was born in the Algerian port city of Oran and was added to UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2022.
Because Earth bulges at the equator, the summit of Ecuador's Chimborazo is the point farthest from the planet's centre.
The Galápagos Islands are named after their giant tortoises, called 'galápagos' in Spanish.
Despite the name, Panama hats come from Ecuador, and weaving them from toquilla straw is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.
Ecuador's name literally means 'Equator' in Spanish.
In 1978, Quito and Kraków became the very first cultural World Heritage Sites declared by UNESCO.
Cotopaxi, Ecuador's second-highest peak at 5,897 metres, is among the highest active volcanoes in the world.
The Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest human-made structure in the world for more than 3,700 years.
The Rosetta Stone, found in Egypt in 1799, became the key to deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs.
In the 1960s, the Abu Simbel temples were cut into 1,036 blocks and moved to higher ground to escape the rising Lake Nasser.
Papyrus was first made in Egypt about 5,000 years ago, and it gave us the word 'paper'.
Wadi Al-Hitan, 'Whale Valley', holds fossils of early whales that still had small hind legs.
The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, links the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea.
Asmara became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017 for its well-preserved modernist architecture.
Asmara's Fiat Tagliero, a petrol station completed in 1938, looks like an aeroplane with huge concrete wings.
At 2,325 metres above sea level, Asmara is the sixth-highest capital city in the world.
Eritrea's narrow-gauge railway from the port of Massawa to Asmara needed 65 bridges and 39 tunnels.
The Dahlak Archipelago in the Red Sea has two large and 124 smaller islands, but only three are permanently inhabited.
Cycling arrived in Eritrea in the Italian era, and in 2015 two Eritreans became the first Black African riders in the Tour de France.
Eritrea has nine recognised ethnic groups, each with its own language.

ESB.capitalNote: Dhekelia has no capital of its own; both Sovereign Base Areas are administered from Episkopi Cantonment in Akrotiri.

funFacts.text: Dhekelia completely surrounds the Cypriot villages of Xylotympou and Ormideia, which form enclaves inside the base area.
Dhekelia and Akrotiri stayed British under the 1960 treaty that made Cyprus independent.
Since 2008 Dhekelia has used the euro, making the base areas the only British territory to officially use it.
The Dhekelia Power Station is split by a British road, so its northern part forms a small extra Cypriot enclave.
Madrid's Sobrino de Botín is listed by Guinness World Records as the oldest restaurant in the world.
On the last Wednesday of August, the town of Buñol holds La Tomatina, a giant street fight with tomatoes.
Spain's national anthem, the Marcha Real, is one of only three national anthems in the world with no official lyrics.
Mount Teide on Tenerife, at 3,715 metres, is Spain's highest peak and an active volcano.
A Coruña's Tower of Hercules, built in the late 1st century, is the only fully preserved Roman lighthouse still used to guide ships.
The cave of Altamira holds Ice Age art, including a ceiling herd of bison; its earliest paintings are about 36,000 years old.
The software behind Skype was created by four Estonians: Ahti Heinla, Priit Kasesalu, Jaan Tallinn and Toivo Annus.
Since 2014, Estonia's e-Residency lets people anywhere get an Estonian digital ID to start a company or bank online.
Estonia has more than 2,300 islands and islets along its Baltic coast.
The Estonian Song Festival has brought together a choir of more than 30,000 singers performing for 80,000 people.
The Kaali craters on Saaremaa island were made by a meteorite impact around 3,500 years ago, in an area where people lived.
Tallinn's Town Hall Pharmacy has been in the same house since the early 1400s, one of Europe's oldest continuously running pharmacies.
Ethiopia's calendar has 13 months, and its year number runs seven or eight years behind the Gregorian calendar.
Wild coffee comes from Ethiopia, and legend tells of a herder whose flock grew lively after nibbling coffee berries.
Lucy, a 3.2-million-year-old human ancestor, was found in Ethiopia in 1974 and named after a Beatles song.
The eleven churches of Lalibela were carved out of solid 'living rock' and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1978.
Dallol in Ethiopia holds the record for the highest average temperature of any inhabited place on Earth.
Ethiopian runner Abebe Bikila won the 1960 Olympic marathon in Rome running barefoot.
Finland may have up to 3.2 million saunas for its 5.5 million people.
Finland has 187,888 lakes larger than five ares (500 square metres).
The sport of wife carrying was first introduced in 1992 in the Finnish town of Sonkajärvi.
Santa Claus Village in Rovaniemi claims to sit on the Arctic Circle, though the real line is about 700 metres further north.
The Linux kernel was created in 1991 by Linus Torvalds, then a student at the University of Helsinki.
Finland's 'everyman's right' lets anyone walk the countryside, camp for a while and pick wild berries and mushrooms.
Finnish sauna culture was added to UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage list in 2020.
The 180th meridian crosses Fiji's island of Taveuni, so part of it lies at 179° east and part at 179° west.
Fiji is made up of more than 330 islands, but only about 110 are permanently inhabited.
Fiji's rugby sevens team won Olympic gold in 2016, the country's first Olympic medal in any event.
In Fiji kava is called yaqona, and a formal yaqona ceremony often accompanies important occasions.
Villages on Fiji's island of Beqa are known for their tradition of fire-walking.
Five species of penguin breed on the Falklands: king, gentoo, rockhopper, Magellanic and macaroni.
More than 400,000 pairs of black-browed albatrosses breed on the Falkland Islands, the majority of the world's population.
Stanley's Whalebone Arch was built in 1933 from the jawbones of two blue whales.
Charles Darwin described the Falklands' boulder-filled 'stone runs' as 'streams of stones' when he visited in 1833 and 1834.
Falkland Islanders call the countryside outside Stanley 'Camp', from the Spanish word 'campo'.
Brunel's steamship SS Great Britain was abandoned in the Falklands in 1937 and towed home to Bristol in 1970.
Thanks to its overseas territories, France uses 12 time zones, more than any other country.
The Tour de France bicycle race was first held in 1903, to boost sales of a newspaper.
The Eiffel Tower was built for the 1889 World's Fair and was due to be dismantled in 1909, but was saved for its use in radio.
Louis Braille, blind since early childhood, first presented his reading system for the blind when he was just 15.
The know-how and culture of the French baguette were added to UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2022.
The Lascaux cave paintings were found in 1940 after a teenager's dog investigated a hole left by an uprooted tree.
The name Faroe is thought to mean 'Sheep Islands', after the many sheep on the archipelago.
Sheep outnumber people on the Faroe Islands: about 70,000 sheep to 54,000 people.
In 2016 Faroe Islanders strapped 360-degree cameras to sheep to make 'Sheep View', because Google Street View hadn't come yet.
From certain angles, the cliffs around the Faroese lake Sørvágsvatn make it look like it floats high above the ocean.
The Eysturoy Tunnel has the world's first undersea roundabout, decorated with metal artwork and lighting effects.
You could only drive to the tiny village of Gásadalur after a tunnel was blasted through the rock in 2004.
The Faroese chain dance is a living tradition: dancers hold hands in a circle while singing old ballads, with no instruments.
On Yap, giant stone discs called rai, the largest 3.6 metres across, are still exchanged in traditional ways.
Nan Madol, a ruined city of 92 artificial islets off Pohnpei, is often called the 'Venice of the Pacific'.
Micronesia is made up of four states, Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae, spread over 607 islands.
Pohnpei is one of the wettest places on Earth, with about 7,600 mm of rain a year in some mountain spots.
In Kosrae legend, the island's mountains are Mahkontowe, the 'Sleeping Lady', who went into the mountains and fell asleep.
About 89% of Gabon is covered by forest, one of the highest forest shares of any country.
At Oklo in Gabon, natural nuclear reactors ran on their own about 2 billion years ago.
Gabon's Loango National Park is called the 'land of surfing hippos', and elephants venture onto its beaches.
In 2002 Gabon set aside 13 national parks at once, covering about a tenth of the country.
Gabon is the stronghold of the mandrill, the largest monkey, whose groups can number in the hundreds.
In 1913 Albert Schweitzer set off to found his famous hospital at Lambaréné, in what is now Gabon.
The London Underground, opened in 1863, was the world's first underground railway.
Big Ben is really the nickname of the Great Bell inside London's clock tower, which is called the Elizabeth Tower.
England's Football Association, formed in 1863, is the oldest football association in the world and drafted the Laws of the Game.
Stonehenge was built in several phases, starting about 3100 BC, more than 5,000 years ago.
The world's first adhesive postage stamp, the Penny Black, was issued in the UK in 1840.
Scotland's Loch Ness holds more water than all the lakes in England and Wales combined.
Georgian winemaking goes back about 8,000 years, and wine is still fermented in big clay jars called qvevri, often buried underground.
Fossils found at Dmanisi in Georgia are about 1.8 million years old, the earliest known human-ancestor remains in Eurasia.
Georgia's unique curly alphabet was added to UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2016.
Traditional Georgian polyphonic singing was among the first traditions UNESCO named a Masterpiece of Oral and Intangible Heritage, in 2001.
At a traditional Georgian feast called a supra, a toastmaster known as the tamada leads the guests through a long series of toasts.
The mountain village of Ushguli, at about 2,100 m, is one of the highest continuously inhabited settlements in Europe, full of medieval tower houses.
Victor Hugo wrote some of his best-known works, including Les Misérables, while living in exile on Guernsey.
The Guernsey cow was bred on the island, and its milk has a golden-yellow tinge from lots of beta-carotene.
The tough knitted fisherman's sweater called a 'guernsey' originated on the island it's named after.
The French painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir visited Guernsey in 1883 and painted the bay and beach of Moulin Huet.
Guernsey's tiny Little Chapel is decorated all over with seashells, pebbles and broken china.
Guernsey issues its own pound coins and banknotes.
Ghana's Lake Volta, created by the Akosombo Dam, is the largest artificial reservoir in the world by surface area.
Colourful kente, Ghana's national cloth, is hand-woven from strips of silk and cotton by Asante and Ewe weavers.
Ghana's Ga people are known for 'fantasy coffins' shaped like lions, crabs, roosters and even aeroplanes.
Cocoa farming in Ghana is traced to Tetteh Quarshie, who planted cocoa seeds at Mampong in 1879.
Kakum National Park has a canopy walkway that hangs about 40 m above the rainforest floor and links seven treetops.
The Prime Meridian (0° longitude) passes through the Ghanaian port city of Tema.
Gibraltar is home to Europe's only wild monkeys, the Barbary macaques that roam the Rock.
Gorham's Cave in Gibraltar was one of the last known homes of the Neanderthals in Europe and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.
The ancient Greeks and Romans saw the Rock of Gibraltar as one of the two Pillars of Hercules.
The biggest chamber of St Michael's Cave inside the Rock is used as a concert hall, thanks to its natural acoustics.
The Rock of Gibraltar is a block of Jurassic limestone riddled with about 55 km of tunnels.
At the Strait of Gibraltar, only about 14 km of sea separates Europe from Africa.
The Niger, Gambia and Senegal rivers all begin in Guinea's highlands.
Guinea's rainy Fouta Djallon highlands feed so many rivers that they're sometimes called the 'water tower of West Africa'.
The Nimba toad of Mount Nimba gives birth to tiny live toadlets instead of laying eggs.
Guinea holds the world's largest reserves of bauxite, the ore used to make aluminium.
Les Ballets Africains, Guinea's national dance company, grew out of a group founded by Guinean artist Fodéba Keïta.
Seen from above, Guadeloupe's two main islands, Basse-Terre and Grande-Terre, form the shape of a butterfly.
La Grande Soufrière on Guadeloupe is an active volcano and the highest peak in the Lesser Antilles, at 1,467 m.
Christopher Columbus named Guadeloupe after Our Lady of Guadalupe, a shrine in the Spanish town of Guadalupe.
The Route du Rhum solo sailing race crosses the Atlantic from Saint-Malo in France to Pointe-à-Pitre in Guadeloupe.
Guadeloupe's Cousteau Reserve around the Pigeon Islets was made famous by ocean explorer Jacques Cousteau, who filmed there.
Guadeloupe is part of France and the EU, so people pay with euros in the middle of the Caribbean.
The Gambia is the smallest country on mainland Africa, a thin strip of land along the lower Gambia River.
The Gambia is surrounded on all sides by Senegal, except for its short Atlantic coastline.
The Senegambian Stone Circles, including Wassu in The Gambia, number over 1,000 and became a UNESCO site in 2006.
At the Kachikally crocodile pool in Bakau, about 80 crocodiles roam freely and visitors can even touch them.
The Gambia is one of only two countries, with the Bahamas, that officially use 'The' in their short name.
The Gambia kept 'The' in its name partly to avoid being confused with Zambia, which became independent around the same time.
Orango Island in Guinea-Bissau's Bijagós Archipelago is known for its rare saltwater hippos.
The Bijagós Archipelago is made up of about 88 islands and islets and became a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve in 1996.
About 5% of the world's green sea turtles nest on tiny Poilão island, the largest green turtle breeding site in Africa.
Cashew nuts are Guinea-Bissau's main export crop.
Gumbe is Guinea-Bissau's best-known music style, and popular songs are almost always sung in Guinea-Bissau Creole.

GNQ.capitalNote: A new planned capital, Ciudad de la Paz, is being built on the mainland.

funFacts.text: Equatorial Guinea is the only country in Africa where Spanish is an official language.
The Equator runs through Equatorial Guinea's waters, just north of its island of Annobón.
The goliath frog, the largest frog in the world, lives near waterfalls in Equatorial Guinea and Cameroon.
Bioko Island is home to rare primates, including the endangered drill and the endemic Pennant's red colobus.
Pico Basilé, a volcano on Bioko Island, is the tallest mountain in Equatorial Guinea at 3,011 m.
Visitors to the remote beaches of Ureka on Bioko Island can watch sea turtles come ashore to nest.
Greece has around 6,000 islands and islets, but only 227 of them are inhabited.
The Olympic flame for every Games is lit at Olympia, Greece, using the Sun's rays and a curved mirror.
Greece's national anthem comes from the 'Hymn to Liberty', a poem with 158 stanzas, though only the first two are used.
The Antikythera mechanism, found in a Greek shipwreck in 1901, is the oldest known example of an analogue computer.
Mount Olympus, the mythical home of the Greek gods, is the highest mountain in Greece at about 2,918 m.
The monasteries of Meteora sit on top of giant natural rock pillars and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988.
Grenada is nicknamed the Island of Spice, and a nutmeg even appears on its national flag.
Molinere Bay in Grenada is home to the world's first underwater sculpture park, created by Jason deCaires Taylor in 2006.
Grenada's Grand Etang Lake and Lake Antoine are crater lakes sitting in two extinct volcanoes.
Kick 'em Jenny, an active underwater volcano, lies on the sea floor just 8 km north of Grenada.
Grenada's national dish, 'oil down', is a stew of breadfruit, salted meat and spices cooked in coconut milk.
About 80% of Greenland is covered by an ice sheet that is more than 3 km thick in places.
Greenland is the world's largest island that is not a continent.
Northeast Greenland National Park is the largest national park in the world.
The Greenland shark can live for centuries, giving it the longest known lifespan of any vertebrate.
Erik the Red supposedly named the icy island 'Greenland' hoping the pleasant name would attract settlers.
Guatemala's currency, the quetzal, is named after its colourful national bird, the resplendent quetzal.
The ancient Maya city of Tikal in Guatemala was used to film the jungle moon Yavin 4 in the first Star Wars film.
Volcán Tajumulco in Guatemala is the highest point in Central America, at about 4,203 m.
Lake Atitlán fills a huge volcanic caldera, is the deepest lake in Central America and has three volcanoes on its southern side.
During Holy Week in Antigua Guatemala, procession routes are covered with carpets made of dyed sawdust, flowers and pine needles.
French Guiana hosts Europe's Spaceport at Kourou, where launching close to the equator gives rockets a boost from Earth's spin.
About 98.9% of French Guiana is covered by forest, much of it untouched rainforest.
Guiana Amazonian Park in French Guiana is the largest national park in the European Union.
French Guiana's Amana Nature Reserve is one of the largest nesting areas in the world for giant leatherback turtles.
French Guiana's carnival is considered the longest in the world, starring disguised dancers called Touloulous.
Guam's motto is 'Where America's Day Begins', because the island is so close to the International Date Line.
The Challenger Deep, the deepest known point of the seabed, lies about 304 km southwest of Guam.
Guam is the largest and southernmost of the Mariana Islands.
Latte stones, ancient stone pillars topped with cap stones, are a symbol of Chamorro identity and appear on Guam's US quarter coin.
The brown tree snake, accidentally brought to Guam after World War II, has caused the extinction of twelve native bird species.
Two Lovers Point on Guam is a 113 m limestone cliff linked to a Chamorro legend of two lovers who tied their hair together and leapt.
Guyana's Kaieteur Falls plunges 226 m, about four and a half times the height of Niagara Falls.
Guyana is the only country in mainland South America where English is the official language.
The name Guyana comes from an Indigenous word meaning 'land of many waters'.
Guyana's national bird, the hoatzin, has chicks with two claws on each wing for clambering through branches.
The giant water lily Victoria amazonica, with leaves up to 3 m across, appears on Guyana's coat of arms.
Pepperpot, a slow-cooked meat stew, is one of Guyana's national dishes and is traditionally served at Christmas.
Hong Kong's Central–Mid-Levels escalator system is 800 m long and carries people 135 m up the hillside.
The Star Ferry has carried passengers across Hong Kong's Victoria Harbour since it was founded in 1888.
Hong Kong's Peak Tram, running since 1888, was the first funicular railway in Asia.
The name Hong Kong translates as 'fragrant harbour'.
Hong Kong-style milk tea is nicknamed 'silk stocking tea' because its tea-stained cloth filter looks like a stocking.
To reach the giant bronze Tian Tan Buddha on Lantau Island, visitors climb 268 steps.
Heard Island's Mawson Peak is an active volcano and the tallest peak on Australian territory outside Antarctica.
Heard Island and McDonald Islands were listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997.
Heard Island lies about 4,100 km southwest of Perth and has been called one of the most remote places on Earth.
Volcanic eruptions made McDonald Island grow from about 1 km² to 2.5 km² between 1994 and 2004.
About a fifth of the world's macaroni penguins breed on Heard Island, alongside king penguins, elephant seals and fur seals.
These are the only sub-Antarctic islands with no species known to have been directly introduced by humans.
The Hieroglyphic Stairway at Copán in Honduras carries the longest known Maya inscription, with about 2,200 glyphs.
In Yoro, Honduras, people celebrate the 'Lluvia de Peces' (rain of fish), when fish are found on the ground after big storms.
The reefs around the Honduran island of Utila teem with marine life, including the elusive whale shark.
The Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve in Honduras protects some of Central America's largest remaining tropical forests and is a UNESCO site.
The Honduran currency, the lempira, is named after Lempira, a 16th-century Lenca ruler.
The Spanish word 'honduras' literally means 'depths'.
The necktie comes from Croatia: the word 'cravat' comes from the neckerchiefs of Croatian soldiers in 1600s France.
The spotty Dalmatian dog breed traces its origins to Dalmatia, a region on Croatia's coast.
Plitvice Lakes National Park has 16 lakes arranged in cascades linked by waterfalls, and has been a UNESCO site since 1979.
Croatian inventor Slavoljub Penkala patented an 'automatic' mechanical pencil in 1906.
The Sea Organ in Zadar, Croatia, plays music using sea waves and tubes hidden under large marble steps.
The hilltop town of Hum in Croatia, with just 52 residents, is considered by some one of the smallest towns in the world.
Haiti's Citadelle Laferrière, perched on a 900 m mountain, is one of the largest fortresses in the Americas.
Haitians eat soup joumou, a pumpkin soup, every New Year's Day, a tradition added to UNESCO's heritage list in 2021.
Artists in Croix-des-Bouquets, Haiti, are famous for a tradition of sculpting iron.
The town of Jacmel in Haiti is famous for its month-long carnival and its colourful papier-mâché masks.
Haiti shares Hispaniola, the second-largest island in the Caribbean, with the Dominican Republic.
Bassin Bleu near Jacmel is Haiti's most famous set of natural deep pools.
The Rubik's Cube was invented in 1974 by Hungarian sculptor and architecture professor Ernő Rubik.
Lake Hévíz is Europe's largest thermal lake; its water stays above 24 °C even on the coldest winter days, so you can bathe all year.
Budapest's Metro Line 1, opened in 1896, was the first electrified underground railway on the European mainland.
Hungarian-born László Bíró patented the first commercially successful ballpoint pen, which is why many Brits still call pens 'biros'.
Lake Balaton in Hungary is the largest lake in Central Europe.
Hungarian scientist Albert Szent-Györgyi won a Nobel Prize for his work on vitamin C, and used Hungarian paprika as a source of it in his experiments.

IDN.capitalNote: A new capital, Nusantara, is under construction on the island of Borneo.

funFacts.text: Komodo dragons, the world's largest living lizards, are found in the wild only on a handful of Indonesian islands.
Indonesia is the world's largest archipelagic country, with between 13,000 and 17,000 islands depending on how you count.
Rafflesia arnoldii, the largest single flower on Earth, grows in the rainforests of Sumatra and Borneo and smells like rotting meat.
Borobudur on the island of Java is the largest Buddhist temple in the world, decorated with 2,672 relief panels.
Kopi luwak, one of the world's priciest coffees, is made from coffee cherries eaten and pooped out by the Asian palm civet.
Tempeh, a protein-rich cake of fermented soybeans, comes from the Indonesian island of Java.
The Isle of Man is home of the Manx cat, a breed best known for having no tail.
The Isle of Man TT motorcycle race has been run on the island's public roads, closed for racing, since 1907.
Tynwald, the Isle of Man's parliament, claims to be the oldest continuous parliament in the world.
The Laxey Wheel, built in 1854 to pump water from mines, is the largest surviving original working waterwheel in the world.
Manx Loaghtan sheep are a rare island breed that usually grow four horns, and sometimes even six.
In 2016 UNESCO gave the Isle of Man the status of a biosphere reserve.
Mawsynram in India's Meghalaya state is reportedly the wettest place on Earth, with nearly 12 m of rain a year on average.
Chess most likely descends from chaturanga, a board game first known from India around the 7th century.
Gir National Park in Gujarat is the only area in Asia where wild Asiatic lions live.
In Meghalaya, people grow 'living root bridges' by guiding the roots of rubber fig trees across streams and rivers.
The English word 'shampoo' comes from the Hindi word 'chāmpo', meaning to knead or massage the head and hair.
The Taj Mahal was commissioned in 1631 by Emperor Shah Jahan as a tomb for his beloved wife Mumtaz Mahal.
The Chagos Archipelago contains the Great Chagos Bank, the largest atoll structure in the world.
The web domain '.io', popular with tech startups and browser games, is officially assigned to the British Indian Ocean Territory.
The Chagos Archipelago is a group of seven atolls with more than 60 tropical islands.
Coconut crabs, the largest land-living arthropods on Earth, live on most of the islands of the Chagos Archipelago.
The remote Chagos islands are perfect undisturbed nesting sites for green and hawksbill sea turtles.
Many Halloween customs come from Samhain, an ancient Gaelic festival from Ireland that marked the end of harvest and the start of winter.
Ireland has no native snakes; legend credits Saint Patrick, but really they never arrived after the last Ice Age.
Newgrange, built around 3100 BC and older than Stonehenge, has an inner chamber that lights up with sunlight at the winter solstice.
The harp is Ireland's emblem and appears on its coins, passports and official seals.
The rocky island of Skellig Michael, with its ancient monks' beehive huts, was used to film the planet Ahch-To in Star Wars.
Arthur Guinness signed a 9,000-year lease for his Dublin brewery at St James's Gate in 1759, for £45 a year.
Iran grows around 90% of the world's saffron, a spice so precious that the best can cost over US$5,000 per kilogram.
Sand in Iran's Lut Desert has been measured by satellite at 70.7 °C, one of the hottest land surfaces ever recorded on Earth.
Ancient Persians built yakhchāls, dome-shaped 'ice houses' that stored ice in the middle of the desert.
The fluffy, long-haired Persian cat's first known ancestors may have come from Khorasan, in what is now eastern Iran and western Afghanistan.
Polo began in ancient Iran as chovgan, which started out as a training game for cavalry.
Nowruz, the Persian New Year, is held on the spring equinox and has been celebrated for over 3,000 years.
Cuneiform, the earliest known writing system, was first developed to write Sumerian in southern Mesopotamia, today's southern Iraq.
The Epic of Gilgamesh, from ancient Mesopotamia in today's Iraq, is the world's oldest surviving example of narrative literature.
Our 60-minute hour and 360-degree circle go back to the base-60 counting system of the ancient Sumerians.
The name Mesopotamia means 'land between rivers', referring to the Tigris and Euphrates that flow through Iraq.
In the marshes of southern Iraq, Marsh Arabs build grand guest houses called mudhif from reeds bent into giant arches.
Masgouf, seasoned grilled carp, is often considered the national dish of Iraq.
Iceland was long one of the only mosquito-free places on Earth, until the first mosquitoes were found there in late 2025.
The English word 'geyser' comes from Geysir, an Icelandic spot where hot springs have been active for about 10,000 years.
Iceland's Althing, established in 930, is considered the oldest legislature in the world.
Icelandic names aren't based on family names; most surnames are a parent's first name plus '-son' or '-dóttir'.
No foreign-born horses may be imported into Iceland, and an Icelandic horse that leaves the country can never come back.
The island of Surtsey rose out of the sea off Iceland's south coast in a volcanic eruption that reached the surface in 1963.

ISR.capitalNote: Israel designates Jerusalem as its capital, but its status is disputed and most countries keep their embassies in Tel Aviv.

funFacts.text: The shores of the Dead Sea are the lowest land on Earth, and its water is so salty that anyone can easily float.
Modern drip irrigation, which saves water by dripping it slowly onto plant roots, was invented in Israel in the 1960s.
Makhtesh Ramon in the Negev Desert is the world's largest makhtesh, a giant crater-like valley carved by erosion, over 40 km long.
Hebrew's revival is unique: no other sacred language has become a national language with millions of native speakers.
An estimated 500 million migrating birds pass through Israel's Hula Valley every year.
The Bahá'í Gardens in Haifa climb Mount Carmel in 19 terraces and became part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008.
Italy completely surrounds two other independent countries: Vatican City and San Marino.
Venice is built on 118 small islands separated by canals and linked by 438 bridges.
The piano was invented in Florence, Italy, by Bartolomeo Cristofori around the year 1700.
Mount Etna in Sicily is one of Europe's tallest active volcanoes and is in an almost constant state of activity.
The Leaning Tower of Pisa started tilting while it was still being built in the 12th century, because of the soft ground beneath it.
The art of the Neapolitan pizza maker, the 'pizzaiuolo', has been on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage since 2017.
Tropical Jamaica sent a bobsleigh team to the 1988 Winter Olympics in Calgary, inspiring the film Cool Runnings.
Reggae music from Jamaica was added to UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage in 2018.
Jamaica's national dish is ackee and saltfish; parts of the ackee fruit are toxic until it ripens and its husk pops open.
Jamaica Blue Mountain Coffee, grown in the island's Blue Mountains, is one of the world's most expensive and sought-after coffees.
Jamaica's national bird, the doctor bird or red-billed streamertail, is a hummingbird found nowhere else on Earth.
The name Jamaica comes from 'Xaymaca', an Indigenous name said to mean 'land of wood and water'.
The Jersey cow, famous for its rich milk that is high in butterfat, was bred on this small Channel Island.
Jersey has one of the largest tidal ranges in the world: the sea can rise and fall up to 12 metres, and at low tide the island nearly doubles in size.
The knitted 'jersey' is named after the island, which became a big exporter of knitted goods in Elizabethan times.
Jersey Royal new potatoes are grown in Jersey and have Protected Designation of Origin status.
Naturalist Gerald Durrell founded Jersey Zoo in 1959, and it has always focused on rare and endangered animals.
The US state of New Jersey is named after the island of Jersey.
Jordan's ancient city of Petra, settled by the Nabataeans in the 4th century BC, is called the 'Rose City' after the colour of the sandstone it is carved from.
Wadi Rum's red desert looks so much like another planet that it stood in for the surface of Mars in the film The Martian.
Mansaf, Jordan's national dish, is lamb cooked in a sauce of fermented dried yogurt, usually served with rice.
The 'Ain Ghazal statues, half-size plaster figures made about 9,000 years ago in what is now Amman, are among the oldest large statues ever found.
Jerash in northern Jordan is one of the best-preserved Greco-Roman cities, nicknamed the 'Pompeii of the Middle East'.
Aqaba is Jordan's only coastal city, and its Red Sea coral reefs make it one of the best diving spots in the world.
When Japan recounted its islands with digital maps in 2023 it found 14,125 of them, more than double the old official figure of 6,852.
Japan's Tōkaidō Shinkansen 'bullet train', opened in 1964, was the world's first high-speed rail line.
Wild snow monkeys at Jigokudani in Nagano warm themselves in natural hot springs during winter.
Nishiyama Onsen Keiunkan, a hot-spring inn founded in 705, is recognised by Guinness as the world's oldest hotel.
Instant noodles were invented in Japan by Momofuku Ando and first went on sale in 1958 as 'Chikin Ramen'.
Mount Fuji, Japan's highest mountain, is an active volcano that last erupted in 1707–1708.
The wild apple Malus sieversii, the main ancestor of the apples we eat today, grows in Kazakhstan and the Tian Shan mountains.
The first satellite, Sputnik 1, and Yuri Gagarin's Vostok 1 both lifted off from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.
Kazakhstan's Charyn Canyon is about 154 km long and, though much smaller than the Grand Canyon, is described as equally impressive.
Kazakh falconers called bürkitshi keep up the tradition of hunting on horseback with golden eagles.
The Kazakh dish beshbarmak means 'five fingers', because it is traditionally eaten with your hands.
The Medeu skating rink near Almaty sits 1,691 m up in the mountains and is the world's largest high-mountain skating rink.
Nairobi National Park lies just 7 km from the city centre, so you can spot lions and giraffes with Nairobi's skyline in the background.
In the Great Migration, over 1.3 million wildebeest plus zebras cross rivers in the Maasai Mara, braving strong currents and crocodiles.
Lake Turkana in northern Kenya is the world's largest permanent desert lake.
Mount Kenya, Africa's second-highest mountain, still has small glaciers even though it lies only 20 km from the equator.
The word 'safari' comes from Swahili, one of Kenya's official languages, and simply means 'journey'.
'Turkana Boy', the most complete early human skeleton ever discovered, was found near Lake Turkana in 1984.
Kyrgyzstan's Lake Issyk-Kul, the world's second-largest mountain lake, sits 1,607 m up yet rarely freezes thanks to its salty water.
The Kyrgyz Epic of Manas has around half a million lines, roughly 20 times longer than Homer's Odyssey and Iliad combined.
The walnut woodland at Arslanbob in southern Kyrgyzstan covers 11,000 hectares, making it the largest walnut grove on Earth.
The yellow sun on Kyrgyzstan's red flag shows a tündük, the round opening at the top of a traditional yurt's roof.
Kyrgyzstan launched the World Nomad Games, featuring sports like kok-boru, where riders fight over a goat carcass.
Almost 90% of Kyrgyzstan lies more than 1,500 m above sea level.
Angkor Wat, listed by Guinness as the largest religious structure in the world, appears on Cambodia's national flag.
The Tonlé Sap river in Cambodia reverses direction when the monsoon rains come, and the lake swells to as much as 16,000 km².
Rare Irrawaddy dolphins, with high, rounded foreheads and no beak, live in the Mekong River in Cambodia, around Kratié.
Guinness World Records lists Khmer, Cambodia's language, as having the most letters of any alphabet: 74.
At Ta Prohm temple, trees grow right out of the ancient stones, and the site starred in the film Lara Croft: Tomb Raider.
Fish amok, one of Cambodia's national dishes, is a fish curry steamed with coconut milk and egg until mousse-like, often served in a banana leaf.
Kiribati's Line Islands sit in the world's earliest time zone, UTC+14, so they are among the first places to greet each New Year.
Kiritimati (Christmas Island) in Kiribati has the largest land area of any atoll with a lagoon in the world.
Kiribati's Phoenix Islands Protected Area was named the world's largest and deepest UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010.
Kiribati's islands straddle both the equator and the 180th meridian, and in 1995 it moved the International Date Line far to the east.
Kiribati is pronounced 'KIRR-i-bass', and its name is the local spelling of 'Gilberts', after the Gilbert Islands.
Kiribati's flag shows a gold frigatebird flying over a gold rising sun, above blue and white waves for the Pacific Ocean.
Alexander Hamilton, one of the Founding Fathers of the United States, was born in Charlestown on the island of Nevis.
Brimstone Hill Fortress on St Kitts, once called the 'Gibraltar of the Caribbean', became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999.
Green monkeys, brought over on ships from West Africa in the late 1600s, now live wild on St Kitts and Nevis.
The St Kitts Scenic Railway runs on a 29 km narrow-gauge line first built to carry sugar cane to the island's sugar mill.
Saint Kitts and Nevis is the smallest sovereign country in the Western Hemisphere, in both area and population.
Nevis gets its name from the Spanish 'Nuestra Señora de las Nieves' (Our Lady of the Snows), perhaps inspired by the white clouds on its peak.
Hangul, the Korean alphabet, was created at King Sejong's court in the 1440s, and South Korea celebrates it with Hangul Day on 9 October.
The Jikji, printed in Korea in 1377, is the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type.
Kimjang, the Korean tradition of making big batches of kimchi for winter, joined UNESCO's cultural heritage list in 2013.
The haenyeo of Jeju Island are women who dive up to 20 m holding their breath, a tradition UNESCO recognised in 2016.
Taekwondo, the Korean martial art famous for its high and spinning kicks, has been an Olympic event since 2000.
Hallasan, a volcano on Jeju Island, is South Korea's highest point at 1,947 m.
Kosovo's flag shows a map of the country, and Cyprus has the only other national flag that does this.
Kosovo has used the euro since 2002, even though it is not part of the eurozone or the EU.
Judoka Majlinda Kelmendi won Kosovo's first ever Olympic medal, a gold, at the 2016 Rio Olympics.
Pristina's giant NEWBORN letters were unveiled with a plan to paint them differently every year on Kosovo's independence anniversary.
Near Pristina, a bear sanctuary gives a home to brown bears that once lived in small cages at restaurants.
Gadime's Marble Cave was discovered in 1966 by a villager who was working in his garden.
The Kuwaiti dinar is the highest-valued currency unit in the world.
The Kuwait Towers, opened in 1979, are covered in about 41,000 steel discs, and two of them are water towers.
Alexander the Great named Kuwait's Failaka Island 'Ikaros', and Greek temples and a fort have been found there.
Mitribah in Kuwait hit 53.9 °C in July 2016, the hottest temperature ever recorded in Asia.
Before oil, Kuwait's economy centred on sea trade, building wooden dhow boats and pearl diving.
Kuwait has no permanent rivers, so it turns seawater into fresh water for drinking.
Laos's Plain of Jars has thousands of ancient stone jars, some up to 3 m tall.
Laos is the only landlocked country in Southeast Asia.
Khone Phapheng Falls on the Mekong River in Laos is the largest waterfall in Southeast Asia.
Laos eats more sticky rice per person than anywhere else: about 171 kg a year each.
Kong Lor Cave in Laos runs about 7 km through a mountain, with the Nam Hin Bun River flowing inside it.
Byblos in Lebanon has been continuously inhabited since about 5000 BC, making it one of the oldest cities in the world.
Royal inscriptions from ancient Byblos show a Phoenician alphabet of 22 letters, an ancestor of many modern alphabets.
