The English word 'Bible' comes from the Greek name of the Lebanese city of Byblos.
The cedar is Lebanon's national emblem, and the ancient Cedars of God forest became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1998.
Jeita Grotto is a nearly 9 km limestone cave system whose lower cave has an underground river you can only visit by boat.
At Baalbek in Lebanon lie three of the largest stone blocks ever quarried in human history.
The name Lebanon comes from an ancient root meaning 'white', after its snow-capped mountains.
Liberia's capital, Monrovia, is named after James Monroe, the fifth president of the United States.
Liberia, which declared independence in 1847, was the first African republic to gain independence.
Liberia's flag has 11 stripes, one for each person who signed its Declaration of Independence.
The shy, nocturnal pygmy hippopotamus lives mainly in Liberia's forests.
Liberia has one of the world's three largest ship registries, so huge numbers of ships fly the Liberian flag.
Liberica, also called Liberian coffee, has beans much larger than Arabica and Robusta.
Libya's Great Man-Made River is the world's largest irrigation project, piping fossil water from an ancient underground aquifer.
Leptis Magna in Libya is among the best-preserved Roman sites in the Mediterranean and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The old town of Ghadames, the 'pearl of the desert', has covered alleyways that shelter people from the summer heat.
In 1922 Al-Aziziya in Libya recorded 58 °C, long thought the world's hottest temperature, until the WMO rejected it in 2012.
Libya's Tadrart Acacus mountains are famous for prehistoric rock art of giraffes, elephants, ostriches and camels.
Cyrene in Libya was founded by Greek colonists around 631 BC and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Saint Lucia's Sulphur Springs is called the Caribbean's only drive-in volcano, and visitors coat themselves in its warm volcanic mud.
The Pitons are two steep volcanic spires in Saint Lucia and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The triangles on Saint Lucia's flag represent the Pitons, the island's twin volcanic peaks.
Saint Lucia is named after Saint Lucy of Syracuse, reportedly because French sailors were shipwrecked there on her feast day.
Saint Lucia has produced two Nobel Prize winners, Arthur Lewis and Derek Walcott, who were both born on 23 January.
The colourful Saint Lucia parrot lives nowhere else in the world and is the island's national bird.
England and France fought 14 times over Saint Lucia, earning it the nickname 'Helen of the West'.
Liechtenstein is one of only two doubly landlocked countries in the world, along with Uzbekistan.
At the 1936 Olympics Liechtenstein found its flag was identical to Haiti's, so it added a golden crown in 1937.
Ivoclar, a global dental company that started out making artificial teeth, is based in Liechtenstein.
Liechtenstein has had no army since 1868, when it was abolished to save money.
In 2011 the whole of Liechtenstein was offered for rent on Airbnb, for $70,000 a night.
Liechtenstein has no currency of its own and uses the Swiss franc.

LKA.capitalNote: Kotte is the official (legislative) capital; Colombo is the commercial capital and largest city.

funFacts.text: Sri Lanka is the world's third-largest tea exporter, and its tea is still sold as 'Ceylon tea'.
Sigiriya is an ancient palace on top of a 180 m granite rock, entered between giant stone lion paws.
True cinnamon, often called Ceylon cinnamon, comes from a tree native to Sri Lanka.
Sri Lanka's town of Ratnapura, meaning 'city of gems', is a centre of mining rubies, sapphires and other gems.
Sri Lanka won the Cricket World Cup in 1996, beating Australia in the final.
Yala National Park in Sri Lanka has one of the highest densities of leopards in the world.
Lesotho is the only country lying entirely above 1,000 m, so it has the highest low point of any nation.
Lesotho is completely surrounded by South Africa; it is the largest of the world's three countries enclosed by another.
Lesotho's flag shows a mokorotlo, the traditional cone-shaped Basotho hat.
Maletsunyane Falls in Lesotho plunges 192 m in a single drop.
Thabana Ntlenyana in Lesotho, at 3,482 m, is the highest mountain in southern Africa.
Through the Lesotho Highlands Water Project, Lesotho's mountain water is sent to South Africa, including Johannesburg.
In 1989 French geographers calculated that the geographical centre of Europe lies in Lithuania, near the village of Girija.
Lithuanian keeps many ancient features of grammar and sound also found in ancient Sanskrit.
Lithuania's basketball team won Olympic bronze in 1992, 1996 and 2000.
The Curonian Spit is a 98 km strip of sand with Europe's highest drifting dunes, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Užupis, an artists' district in Vilnius, declared itself an independent republic with its own constitution on 1 April 1997.
Vilnius Old Town is one of the largest surviving medieval old towns in Northern Europe and a UNESCO site.
In 2020 Luxembourg became the first country to make all public transport free nationwide.
Luxembourg is the world's only remaining sovereign grand duchy.
The Schengen Agreement, which removed border checks across Europe, was signed on a boat on the Moselle near Schengen, Luxembourg.
About 17 km of underground casemate tunnels still run beneath Luxembourg City, partly carved into the rock.
Robert Schuman, one of the founding fathers of the European Union, was born in Luxembourg City in 1886.
Luxembourg has three administrative languages: Luxembourgish, French and German.
About half of Latvia is covered in forest.
Art Nouveau makes up a third of the buildings in central Riga, the highest concentration of any city in the world.
Riga Central Market is housed in giant hangars that were originally built for German Zeppelin airships.
Ventas Rumba in Latvia is the widest waterfall in Europe, about 249 m across.
Latvia's Song and Dance Festival brings together about 40,000 performers and is on a UNESCO heritage list.
On Jāņi, Latvia's midsummer festival, people wear flower and oak-leaf crowns and sing through the night until sunrise.
The Macau Tower holds the Guinness record for the highest commercial bungee jump facility on a building, at about 233 m.
The Historic Centre of Macau, blending Chinese and Portuguese cultures, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005.
The Macau Grand Prix has been raced on the city's street circuit since 1954.
Macau is the most densely populated region in the world.
Macau's Portuguese tarts have a flaky crust and caramelised top, and making them is part of Macau's cultural heritage.
Cotai, home to many big resorts, was built on land reclaimed from the sea between Macau's islands of Taipa and Coloane.
The island has been shared by France and the Netherlands since a 1648 treaty, and you can cross the border freely.
Legend says the border was set by a Frenchman with wine and a Dutchman with gin walking around the island in opposite directions.
Pic Paradis, at 424 m on the French side, is the highest point on the island of Saint Martin.
Columbus actually gave the name 'Saint Martin' to Nevis in 1493; it moved to this island through a mix-up.
The University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, founded around 859, is cited as the world's oldest continually operating higher-learning institution.
The old medina of Fez, Fes el Bali, is a huge car-free urban area of about 300 hectares.
Chefchaouen in Morocco's Rif Mountains is nicknamed the 'Blue City' for its buildings in shades of blue.
In Morocco, goats sometimes climb high into argan trees to reach the fruit.
Mount Toubkal, at 4,167 m, is the highest peak in North Africa and the Arab world.
In 1777 Morocco became the first country in the world to recognise the newly independent United States.
Monaco's Grand Prix has been raced through the narrow streets of Monte Carlo since 1929.
Monaco is the second-smallest country in the world, after Vatican City.
Monaco's Oceanographic Museum towers 85 m above the sea on a sheer cliff, and Jacques Cousteau directed it for 31 years.
Hollywood star Grace Kelly became Princess of Monaco when she married Prince Rainier III in 1956.
Monaco's Fontvieille district was built in the 1970s on land claimed from the sea.
Monte Carlo, home of the famous casino, was named in honour of Prince Charles III of Monaco.
Moldova's Mileștii Mici holds the Guinness record for the world's largest wine collection, in cellars stretching about 200 km.
Cricova in Moldova has an underground 'wine city' with 120 km of roads named after the wines stored there.
Moldova celebrates National Wine Day on the first weekend of October every year.
Orheiul Vechi in Moldova sits on a narrow river bend, with cave chapels and a hilltop monastery still home to monks.
A point of the Struve Geodetic Arc, a 19th-century chain used to measure the size and shape of the Earth, is in Moldova.
On 1 March, Moldovans give each other red-and-white mărțișor threads to welcome spring, a tradition on UNESCO's list since 2017.
Over 90% of Madagascar's wildlife is found nowhere else on Earth.
Lemurs are found in the wild only on Madagascar.
Madagascar is the fourth-largest island in the world.
Six of the world's eight baobab tree species grow only in Madagascar.
Tsingy de Bemaraha's razor-sharp limestone 'forests' get their name from a Malagasy word for 'where one cannot walk barefoot'.
Madagascar is the world's top vanilla grower, producing 42% of the world's raw vanilla in 2023.
About half of the world's chameleon species live only in Madagascar.
The Maldives is the world's lowest-lying country: its highest natural point is only about 2.4 m above sea level.
The Maldives is made up of 1,192 coral islands grouped into 26 atolls.
Hanifaru Bay in the Maldives sees some of the world's largest gatherings of manta rays, which come to feed on plankton.
Ithaa, a restaurant 5 m below sea level in the Maldives, billed itself as the world's first undersea restaurant.
Cowrie shells traded from the Maldives were once used as money across Asia and parts of East Africa.
The Maldives is the smallest country in Asia.
Corn (maize) was first domesticated in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago from a wild grass called teosinte.
The Great Pyramid of Cholula is the largest pyramid in the world by volume, bigger even than Egypt's Great Pyramid of Giza.
Monarch butterflies fly up to about 4,800 km from Canada and the USA to spend the winter in the forests of central Mexico.
Vanilla comes from an orchid first found in Mesoamerica, including Mexico, and the Totonac people were among the first to grow it.
The axolotl, a smiling salamander that can regrow lost limbs, is native only to the lakes of Xochimilco and Chalco near Mexico City.
The Chicxulub crater, buried under Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, was made by the asteroid linked to the extinction of the dinosaurs.
Marshallese navigators made 'stick charts' from coconut-frond ribs and shells to map ocean swells around the islands.
The bikini swimsuit, launched in Paris in 1946, was named after Bikini Atoll in the Marshall Islands.
Kwajalein Atoll has 97 islands and islets ringing one of the world's largest lagoons, about 2,174 km² of water.
The Marshall Islands are made up of 29 coral atolls, 5 main islands and over 1,200 tiny islets in the Pacific Ocean.
In 2011 the Marshall Islands set aside nearly 2 million km² of ocean as the world's largest shark sanctuary.
The islands are named after British sea captain John Marshall, who explored the region in 1788.
Lake Ohrid, about 1.36 million years old, is considered Europe's oldest lake and has more than 300 species found nowhere else.
Water from Lake Prespa trickles through underground channels in the limestone mountains to reach Lake Ohrid.
The Lake Ohrid region is a UNESCO World Heritage Site listed for both its natural and its cultural value.
Famous 'Ohrid pearls' are handmade using a secret coating made from the scales of the plasica, a small fish from Lake Ohrid.
Mother Teresa was born in Skopje in 1910, and a memorial house in her honour opened there in 2009.
Tavče gravče, beans baked in a clay pot with onion and red pepper, is considered North Macedonia's national dish.
The Great Mosque of Djenné is the world's largest mud-brick building, and the whole town helps re-plaster it at a yearly festival.
Mansa Musa of the Mali Empire gave away so much gold in Egypt that its value there stayed low for at least twelve years.
Some 350,000 old Timbuktu manuscripts, on art, medicine, philosophy and science, were rescued and carried to safety.
The Dogon people live in dozens of villages along the 150 km-long Bandiagara Escarpment, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1989.
Mali's desert elephants of the Gourma region make the longest known elephant migration circuit in the world.
West African griots, or jalis, play the kora, a harp-lute with 21 strings that is played in Mali and its neighbours.
Malta's Ġgantija temples, built from around 3600 BC, are older than the pyramids of Egypt.
The Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum is an underground prehistoric burial complex cut into solid rock about 5,000 years ago.
Maltese is the only Semitic language that is an official language of the European Union, and it is written in the Latin alphabet.
Valletta packs 320 monuments into just 0.55 km², making it one of the most concentrated historic areas in the world.
Popeye Village in Malta was built as the film set for the 1980 movie 'Popeye' and is now a small fun park.
Pastizzi, flaky diamond-shaped pastries filled with ricotta or curried peas, are a much-loved traditional Maltese snack.
More than 2,000 ancient temples and pagodas still dot the plains of Bagan in Myanmar.
Fishermen on Inle Lake row standing on one leg with the other wrapped around the oar, so they can see over the reeds.
Many people in Myanmar wear thanaka, a paste made from ground tree bark, on their faces as make-up and protection from sunburn.
Chinlone is a traditional Myanmar sport where players keep a woven rattan ball in the air without using their hands.
Mohinga, a fish soup with rice noodles, is the national dish of Myanmar and a favourite breakfast.
Hkakabo Razi, about 5,881 m high in northern Myanmar, is the highest mountain in Southeast Asia.

MNE.capitalNote: Cetinje holds the constitutional title of Old Royal Capital and hosts the presidential residence.

funFacts.text: Montenegro's Tara River Canyon, up to about 1,300 m deep, is the deepest canyon in continental Europe.
The name Montenegro means 'Black Mountain', after the dark evergreen forests that once covered Mount Lovćen.
The Bay of Kotor is a ria: the drowned valley of a vanished river that once flowed down from Mount Orjen.
Our Lady of the Rocks is an artificial islet in the Bay of Kotor, built up by sailors dropping rocks and sinking old ships.
Lake Skadar, shared with Albania, is the largest lake in the Balkans and home to some of Europe's last pelicans.
An olive tree near Bar, called Stara Maslina ('Old Olive'), is said to be more than 2,000 years old.
The first dinosaur eggs recognised by scientists were found in Mongolia in 1923 by an American Museum of Natural History team.
Mongolia's Naadam festival celebrates the 'three games of men': wrestling, horse racing and archery.
Przewalski's horses, once extinct in the wild, have been reintroduced to Mongolia since 1992.
In western Mongolia, Kazakh eagle hunters ride on horseback with golden eagles to hunt foxes and hares in winter.
Ulaanbaatar is the coldest national capital in the world, with January nights dropping to between -36 and -40°C.
Rare wild Bactrian camels, a separate species from the domestic ones, still survive in Mongolia's Gobi Desert.
The nearby Mariana Trench, named after these islands, is the deepest ocean trench on Earth.
Ancient islanders built houses on stone pillars called latte stones, and the House of Taga on Tinian has the largest known one.
Besides English, the Northern Mariana Islands have Chamorro and Carolinian as official languages.
The volcano on Anatahan island had its first recorded eruption in May 2003.
The Micronesian megapode, found in the Northern Marianas, lays its eggs in mounds and uses volcanic heat to incubate them.
The Mariana fruit dove, a small green dove with a red forehead, is the official bird of the Northern Mariana Islands.
Mozambique's Bazaruto Archipelago is home to about 120 dugongs, or 'sea cows', the country's largest remaining population.
Mozambique takes its name from the small Island of Mozambique, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Tofo in Mozambique is one of the few places on Earth where whale sharks and manta rays live all year round.
Lake Cahora Bassa, created by a dam on the Zambezi River, is Africa's fourth-largest artificial lake.
Fiery peri-peri sauce, made with African bird's eye chillies, was developed by the Portuguese, and its modern use began in Mozambique.
Mozambique's coastline stretches about 2,470 km along the Indian Ocean.
The Richat Structure, a 40 km-wide eroded rock dome in the Sahara, is often called the 'Eye of Africa'.
Mauritania's iron ore trains are up to 3 km long, among the longest and heaviest trains in the world.
Over two million migrating shorebirds spend the winter in Banc d'Arguin National Park on Mauritania's coast.
The ancient desert town of Chinguetti is famous for its medieval libraries of old manuscripts.
Mauritania's ouguiya is one of only two currencies in the world not divided into units of 100: one ouguiya is 5 khoums.
Ben Amera in Mauritania is Africa's largest monolith and the second-largest in the world after Uluru.

MSR.capitalNote: Plymouth is still the official capital but was abandoned after volcanic eruptions in the 1990s; government now sits in Brades.

funFacts.text: Montserrat is nicknamed the 'Emerald Isle of the Caribbean' because of its Irish links and its likeness to Ireland.
Montserrat is the only place outside Ireland where St Patrick's Day is a national holiday.
Customs officers on Montserrat stamp a shamrock in visitors' passports, a nod to the island's Irish heritage.
AIR Studios Montserrat, opened by Beatles producer George Martin in 1979, hosted stars like Paul McCartney, The Police and Dire Straits.
The Montserrat oriole, a black-and-orange-yellow songbird found only on Montserrat, is the island's national bird.
The 'mountain chicken' is not a bird but one of the world's largest frogs, now found only on Montserrat and Dominica.
Columbus named the island in 1493 after the Virgin of Montserrat, whose monastery sits on a jagged mountain near Barcelona.
Joséphine, Napoleon's first wife and Empress of the French, was baptised in Les Trois-Îlets on Martinique.
Martinique's rhum agricole is distilled from freshly squeezed sugarcane juice, and its AOC quality label is unique to the island.
Martinique's old Indigenous name, Madinina, is said to mean 'island of flowers'.
The famous poet Aimé Césaire was born in Martinique, and the island's airport is named after him.
As part of France, Martinique is in the European Union and uses the euro, even though it is in the Caribbean.
The volcanoes and forests of Mount Pelée and the northern peaks of Martinique became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.
Mauritius was the only home of the dodo, a flightless bird that became a famous symbol of extinction.
Seen from the air, the sea off Le Morne Brabant looks like it has an 'underwater waterfall'.
At Chamarel in Mauritius, the Seven Coloured Earths are dunes of sand in red, brown, violet, green, blue, purple and yellow.
Mauritius's 1847 'Post Office' stamps, including the famous Blue Mauritius, are among the rarest stamps in the world.
In 1974 only four Mauritius kestrels were known in the wild, but conservation work brought them back to about 400 birds.
Sega, a lively Mauritian music and dance born among the island's enslaved people, is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.
Lake Malawi has more fish species than any other lake on Earth, and its many cichlids are found nowhere else.
Malawi is nicknamed 'The Warm Heart of Africa' because of the loving nature of its people.
Explorer David Livingstone called Lake Malawi the 'Lake of Stars' after seeing the lanterns of fishermen's boats at night.
The Mulanje cedar, Malawi's national tree, grows naturally only on the Mulanje Massif.
Gule Wamkulu, a masked dance of the Chewa people, was named a UNESCO Masterpiece of Intangible Heritage in 2005.
Malawi's Nyika Plateau blooms with more than 200 kinds of orchids, especially during the rains from January to April.

MYS.capitalNote: Putrajaya is the administrative centre and seat of the federal government.

funFacts.text: Kuala Lumpur's Petronas Towers were the world's tallest buildings from 1998 to 2004 and are still the tallest twin towers.
Rafflesia, giant flowers that smell of rotting flesh, grow in Malaysia; some kinds can be more than 1 m wide.
The Sarawak Chamber in Gunung Mulu National Park is the largest known cave chamber in the world by area.
Nepenthes rajah, a giant pitcher plant from Mount Kinabalu in Sabah, has traps big enough to catch rats.
The Sepilok Orangutan Rehabilitation Centre in Sabah helps orphaned orangutans learn to live in the wild.
Nasi lemak, rice cooked in coconut milk and served with sambal, anchovies, peanuts and egg, is Malaysia's national dish.
Mayotte is surrounded by one of the world's largest and deepest lagoons, partly enclosed by a rare double barrier reef.
Women on Mayotte often wear masonjoany, a sandalwood paste face mask that works as both sunscreen and decoration.
Ylang-ylang, a flower used in famous French perfumes like Chanel N°5, has become an icon of Mayotte.
Lake Dziani on Petite-Terre fills the crater of an ancient volcano that went extinct about 500,000 years ago.
Brown lemurs, brought to the island by people long ago, now live wild on Mayotte.
Green sea turtles nest on Mayotte all year round; about 1,500 come ashore each year at Grande Saziley beach alone.
The Hoba meteorite, the largest known intact meteorite at over 60 tonnes, still lies where it fell in Namibia.
The Namib may be the oldest desert in the world, dry for some 55 to 80 million years.
In Deadvlei, camel thorn trees that died 600–700 years ago still stand on a white clay pan among giant dunes.
Welwitschia, a strange desert plant with only two leaves that never stop growing, may live for up to 2,000 years.
Mysterious 'fairy circles', bare round patches 2–12 m wide, dot the grasslands along a 2,400 km strip of the Namib.
Cape Cross on Namibia's Skeleton Coast is home to one of the largest Cape fur seal colonies in the world.
New Caledonia's national bird, the kagu, has a call that sounds like a bark and can be heard a mile away.
New Caledonia's lagoon, about 24,000 km², is among the largest in the world and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008.
Amborella, a shrub found only in New Caledonia, belongs to the oldest surviving branch of the flowering plant family tree.
New Caledonian crows are famous for making and using their own tools, like hooks made from twigs.
The crested gecko from New Caledonia was thought to be extinct until it was rediscovered in 1994.
The 'Heart of Voh' is a natural clearing in a mangrove swamp shaped just like a heart when seen from the air.
Nigersaurus, a dinosaur discovered in Niger, had more than 500 teeth, each replaced about every 14 days.
The Tree of Ténéré in Niger was once called the most isolated tree on Earth, until a truck knocked it down in 1973.
At the Gerewol festival, young Wodaabe men paint their faces and dance while young women judge their beauty.
The minaret of the Agadez mosque, about 27 m tall, is the tallest structure ever built of mud brick.
Niger has the last self-sustaining herd of wild West African giraffes, which roam near the village of Kouré.
The Dabous giraffes, 6 m tall and carved 6,000–8,000 years ago in Niger's Aïr Mountains, are the largest known animal rock carvings.
Many Norfolk Islanders descend from the Bounty mutineers, whose Pitcairn-born families moved here in 1856.
The tall Norfolk Island pine is native to the island and is pictured on its flag.
Many islanders speak Norf'k, a language mixing 18th-century English and Tahitian.
Norfolk Island is one of the few places outside North America that celebrates Thanksgiving.
So few surnames are used on Norfolk Island that the phone book lists people by nicknames like Carrots, Possum and Pumpkin.
Kingston and Arthur's Vale on Norfolk Island are part of the Australian Convict Sites on UNESCO's World Heritage List.
In 2009 UNESCO rated Nigeria's Nollywood the world's second-biggest film industry by output, after India's.
Nigeria's Nok culture made terracotta sculptures 2,000 to 2,900 years ago, some of the oldest in West Africa.
The Cross River gorilla, the world's rarest great ape, lives in the forested hills on the Nigeria–Cameroon border.
In 1996 Nigeria became the first African country to win the Olympic gold medal in football, beating Argentina 3–2 in the final.
Zuma Rock, a giant natural monolith just west of Abuja, is so famous that it appears on Nigeria's 100 naira banknote.
Nigeria's Sukur was Africa's first cultural landscape added to UNESCO's World Heritage List, in 1999.
Bull sharks live in freshwater Lake Nicaragua, and sharks tagged in the lake have later been caught out in the open ocean.
Lake Nicaragua is the largest freshwater lake in Central America.
Ometepe, an island in Lake Nicaragua, is made of two volcanoes, Concepción and Maderas, joined by a low isthmus.
Cerro Negro first appeared in 1850, making it the youngest volcano in Central America.
At Cerro Negro visitors go 'volcano boarding', sliding down the side of the volcano on a wooden sled.
Unlike most of Latin America, Nicaragua's most popular sport is baseball rather than football.
León Viejo, founded in 1524, is the only 16th-century colonial city in the Americas never altered by later city planning, and is UNESCO-listed.
In March 2020 Niue became the world's first dark-sky country, protecting its starry night skies.
Niue is one of the world's largest coral islands, nicknamed 'The Rock' from its old name 'Rock of Polynesia'.
In 2003 Niue became the first country to provide state-funded wireless internet to all its inhabitants.
Niue's internet domain .nu is popular in Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands because 'nu' means 'now' in their languages.
Niue has issued legal-tender collector coins showing Star Wars characters in colour.
The katuali, or flat-tail sea snake, is found only in the waters around Niue.
Jan Mayen's Beerenberg is the world's northernmost active volcano above sea level, and its ice cap feeds about twenty glaciers.
Jan Mayen is named after Dutch captain Jan Jacobszoon May; the island's first verified discoveries came in 1614.
In its whaling heyday, about 200 men lived on Jan Mayen each season at six temporary whaling stations.
Jan Mayen has no permanent residents; only staff of the Norwegian Armed Forces and Meteorological Institute live there.
An Austro-Hungarian expedition spent a whole year on Jan Mayen during the first International Polar Year, 1882–83.
Beerenberg erupted in 1970, 1973 and most recently in 1985.
About a quarter (26%) of the Netherlands lies below sea level, much of it reclaimed land called polders.
The Netherlands has about 18 million bicycles, around 1.3 for every person old enough to ride.
During Dutch 'tulip mania' a single tulip bulb could cost more than five houses, in history's first recorded speculative bubble.
The Flevopolder, reclaimed from the sea, is by some definitions the largest artificial island in the world.
The 19 windmills of Kinderdijk, built around 1740 to drain the land, have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997.
In 1608 Dutch spectacle-maker Hans Lipperhey applied for a patent on a telescope, the earliest written record of one.

NLY.capitalNote: Each island has its own capital: Kralendijk (Bonaire), Oranjestad (Sint Eustatius) and The Bottom (Saba).

funFacts.text: Saba's airport runway, only about 400 m long, is reputed to be the shortest commercial runway in the world.
Mount Scenery on Saba is the highest point in the whole Kingdom of the Netherlands, at 870 m.
Saba's 'The Road' was built by hand by islanders from 1938 to 1958, even though Dutch and Swiss engineers thought it couldn't be done.
Bonaire National Marine Park protects the reefs around the entire island, making Bonaire a famous diving destination.
Bonaire is home to one of only four nesting grounds of the Caribbean flamingo.
On 16 November 1776 Sint Eustatius fired the 'First Salute', the first recognition of the United States by a foreign power.
Salmon sushi only took off in Japan after parasite-free Norwegian salmon was introduced there in the late 1980s.
The handy cheese slicer was invented by Norwegian Thor Bjørklund in 1925.
The Nobel Peace Prize is presented in Oslo; it is the only Nobel Prize not presented in Stockholm.
Every year since 1947, Oslo has given London a giant Christmas tree for Trafalgar Square as thanks for wartime help.
Norway's Lærdal Tunnel is 24.5 km long, the longest road tunnel in the world.
Sondre Norheim from Telemark is known as the father of Telemark skiing and a pioneer of modern skiing.
Nepal has the only national flag that isn't rectangular: two triangles forming a double pennant, taller than it is wide.
Nepal is home to eight of the world's ten highest mountains, including Mount Everest.
Nepal's clock is 5 hours 45 minutes ahead of UTC, one of only three time zones with a 45-minute offset.
Lumbini in Nepal, where the Buddha was born, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997.
Chitwan National Park has Nepal's largest population of greater one-horned rhinos and is one of the best tiger habitats in the world.
The Kathmandu Valley contains seven World Heritage sites, including three royal Durbar Squares and Swayambhunath.

NRU.capitalNote: Nauru has no official capital; government offices are in Yaren District.

funFacts.text: Nauru is the world's third-smallest country, with only about 30 km of road.
Nauru's wealth came from phosphate, which formed from guano deposited by seabirds.
British sea captain John Fearn named Nauru 'Pleasant Island' in 1798 because of its attractive appearance.
On Nauru's flag the gold stripe is the Equator, and the 12 points of the star stand for the island's 12 original tribes.
Australian rules football became Nauru's national sport after independence in 1968.
The Nauru reed warbler lives nowhere else on Earth and is the only songbird (passerine) found on the island.
Svalbard's Global Seed Vault, kept cold by permafrost, stores backup copies of over 1.3 million seed samples from around the world.
Anyone leaving Longyearbyen is advised to carry a rifle for protection against polar bears.
Longyearbyen no longer buries bodies, because it was found they don't decompose in the permafrost.
The Svalbard reindeer is a small, short-legged reindeer found only on Svalbard.
In May 1926 the airship Norge set off from King's Bay (Ny-Ålesund) in Svalbard and flew over the North Pole.
In Longyearbyen the midnight sun shines around the clock from 20 April to 23 August.
Before people arrived, New Zealand's only land mammals were a few species of bat.
In 1893 New Zealand became the first nation where all women had the right to vote in parliamentary elections.
The Kawarau Gorge Suspension Bridge near Queenstown was the world's first commercial bungy jumping site.
A hill in Hawke's Bay has an 85-letter Māori name, possibly the longest place name in the world.
New Zealand's kākāpō is the world's only flightless parrot, and also the heaviest.
Kiwi eggs are among the largest in the bird world compared to the size of the bird.
Oman's 'Land of Frankincense' in Dhofar, with ports key to the medieval incense trade, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.
Oman's aflaj, ancient gravity-fed channels that carry water to villages and farms, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2006.
Bahla Fort, built of mud bricks and straw, was Oman's first UNESCO-listed fort, in 1987.
Ras al Jinz is a nature reserve for green turtles and one of Oman's largest turtle nesting sites.
Each summer the khareef monsoon soaks the Dhofar mountains around Salalah in rain and fog.
Musandam's rugged coast looks like the glacier-carved fjords of polar regions, with the sea filling its valleys.
Mohenjo-daro, built around 2500 BC in Sindh, was one of the world's earliest major cities and had a drainage system along its streets.
K2, the world's second-highest mountain, rises in the Karakoram range, partly in Pakistan's Gilgit-Baltistan.
Sialkot is the world's largest maker of hand-sewn footballs, and a local firm has made official World Cup match balls since 2014.
In Pakistan's truck art, Karachi-style lorries sparkle with flashing bulbs, glass and mirrors, with chains dangling from the bumpers.
The Khewra Salt Mine is the world's second-largest salt mine, famous for pink salt often sold as Himalayan salt.
The Indus river dolphin, Pakistan's national mammal, is effectively blind because its eyes have no lens.
The Panama Canal's locks lift ships 26 metres (85 ft) up to the canal's main level at Gatun Lake.
When it was built for the Panama Canal, Gatun Lake was the largest artificial lake in the world.
The Darién Gap in Panama is the only break in the Pan-American Highway, which otherwise runs from Alaska to Argentina.
About 3 million years ago the Isthmus of Panama formed, linking North and South America and letting animals cross between them.
Guna women of Panama make molas, colourful cloth panels sewn in layers and worn on their traditional blouses.
The Panamanian golden frog, found only in Panama, is a national symbol and even appears on lottery tickets.
Most Pitcairn islanders descend from nine HMS Bounty mutineers and twelve Tahitian women, who settled there in 1790.
Every year on Bounty Day, 23 January, Pitcairners burn a model of the Bounty, which the mutineers set ablaze in 1790.
Uninhabited Henderson Island is a UNESCO-listed raised coral atoll, one of the last two whose ecosystems are still largely untouched by humans.
Many islanders speak Pitkern, a creole of 18th-century English with elements of Tahitian.
Pitcairn's steep cliffs mean the island can only be reached by boat, landing at Bounty Bay.
In 2015 the Pitcairn Islands created a marine reserve covering its whole sea zone, over 834,000 km² of ocean.
Potatoes were first domesticated around Lake Titicaca in southern Peru and Bolivia, and about 3,000 varieties grow in the Andes.
Machu Picchu, a 15th-century Inca citadel, was brought to world attention in 1911 by Hiram Bingham.
The Nazca Lines are giant drawings of animals, plants and shapes in Peru's desert soil, some best seen from the air.
On Lake Titicaca, the Uros live on about 120 floating islands they build from bundles of totora reeds.
Peru's Colca Canyon is about 3,270 m deep, one of the deepest canyons in the world.
Ceviche, raw fish marinated in lemon or lime juice, is considered Peru's national dish.
The Spratly Islands are a scatter of islands, islets, cays and more than 100 reefs in the South China Sea.
All the natural land of the Spratly Islands put together adds up to less than 2 km².
The islands are named after British whaling captain Richard Spratly, who sighted Spratly Island in 1843.
The poorly charted northeast of the Spratlys is called 'Dangerous Ground', and sailors are told to avoid it.
Taiping Island (Itu Aba) is the largest naturally occurring island in the Spratlys, and it has freshwater wells.
The Philippines is made up of about 7,641 islands.
The Banaue Rice Terraces were carved into the mountains largely by hand by ancestors of the Igorot people.
Bohol's Chocolate Hills are at least 1,260 grassy mounds that turn chocolate-brown in the dry season.
The Philippine tarsier is one of the smallest primates and has the largest eye-to-body weight ratio of any mammal.
The Philippine eagle, the national bird, is the largest living eagle in the world by length and wing surface.
On Palawan, the Puerto Princesa Subterranean River flows 8.2 km underground through caves before reaching the sea.
In 2009 Palau announced the world's first shark sanctuary.
In Palau's Jellyfish Lake, snorkellers swim among millions of golden jellyfish whose stings are too weak to harm people.
Palau's Rock Islands, 250 to 300 mostly mushroom-shaped islets, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012.
Visitors to Palau get the 'Palau Pledge', a promise to protect the islands, stamped in their passport.
On 1 January 2020 Palau became the first country to ban sunscreens containing chemicals thought to harm coral reefs.
Yap's giant stone money discs (rai) were mostly quarried in Palau and carried home by canoe or bamboo raft.
Papua New Guinea is the most linguistically diverse country in the world, with about 840 living languages.
A golden Raggiana bird-of-paradise appears on Papua New Guinea's flag as a symbol of its tribal culture.
The hooded pitohui of New Guinea is one of the few known poisonous birds, with toxin in its skin and feathers.
Queen Alexandra's birdwing, the world's largest butterfly, lives only in the forests of Papua New Guinea's Oro Province.
At UNESCO-listed Kuk Swamp, people were draining land to farm about 9,000 years ago.
Rugby league is Papua New Guinea's national sport and its most popular one.
Miners at the Wieliczka Salt Mine carved four chapels out of rock salt, and St Kinga's Chapel even has salt-crystal chandeliers.
Marie Curie, born in Warsaw, was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the only person to win in two different sciences.
Nicolaus Copernicus, who put the Sun rather than Earth at the centre of the universe, was born in Toruń in 1473.
Białowieża Forest, one of Europe's last primeval forests, is home to more than 800 European bison.
Malbork Castle, built by the Teutonic Knights, is the largest castle in the world by land area.
Every hour a trumpeter in Kraków's St Mary's Church plays the Hejnał, a tune that ends abruptly before it's finished.
Puerto Rico has three of the Caribbean's seven year-round bioluminescent bays, including Puerto Mosquito on Vieques.
Mosquito Bay on Vieques holds the Guinness World Record as the brightest bioluminescent bay on Earth.
El Yunque is the only tropical rainforest in the U.S. National Forest System.
The tiny coquí frog is named after the loud 'co-quí' call males make at night, and it's an unofficial symbol of Puerto Rico.
The piña colada originated in Puerto Rico, which proclaimed it its official drink in 1978.
Puerto Rico's Arecibo Telescope, a 305 m dish, was the world's largest single-aperture telescope for 53 years.
Work on the El Morro fortress in Old San Juan began in 1539, and it became part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983.
Mount Paektu, on the China–North Korea border, is a volcano whose caldera holds a big crater lake called Heaven Lake.
Pyongyang's Rungrado 1st of May Stadium, with a roof shaped like a magnolia blossom, is the world's second-largest stadium.
The pyramid-shaped Ryugyong Hotel has 105 floors; construction began in 1987, but it has never opened.
The Pyongyang Metro is among the deepest in the world, with tracks over 110 m underground, so its stations double as bomb shelters.
Pyongyang naengmyeon, cold noodles mainly made from buckwheat, comes from the capital city.
The Complex of Koguryo Tombs, with brightly coloured wall paintings, became North Korea's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004.
Portugal produces about half of the world's cork, harvested from cork oak bark without cutting the trees down.
Cabo da Roca, near Lisbon, is the westernmost point of continental Europe.
The pastel de nata custard tart was created by monks at the Jerónimos Monastery in Belém, Lisbon.
An underwater canyon gives Nazaré giant waves; in 2020 Sebastian Steudtner surfed a world-record 26.2 m wave there.
Bertrand bookshop in Lisbon, founded in 1732, is recognised by Guinness as the world's oldest operating bookshop.
In 1756 the Douro Valley, home of port wine, became the world's first wine region with a formal demarcation.
More than 90% of Paraguayans speak the indigenous Guaraní language alongside Spanish.
Paraguay's flag is the only national flag with a different design on each side: a star on the front, a lion on the back.
The Itaipu Dam on the Paraná River, shared with Brazil, is one of the world's biggest hydroelectric dams by energy produced.
In 2020 UNESCO added Paraguay's tereré, an ice-cold yerba mate drink, to its Intangible Cultural Heritage list.
The Chacoan peccary was known only from fossils and thought extinct until it was found alive in the Gran Chaco in 1971.
The ruins of the Jesuit Missions of La Santísima Trinidad and Jesús de Tavarangue are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

PSX.capitalNote: East Jerusalem is the proclaimed capital; Ramallah serves as the administrative centre.

funFacts.text: Jericho is among the oldest cities in the world, and at 258 m below sea level it's the lowest city on Earth.
Bethlehem's Church of the Nativity was the first Palestinian site added to the UNESCO World Heritage List, in 2012.
Nablus is famous for knafeh, a pastry layered with white Nabulsi cheese and soaked in sweet syrup.
Palestinian embroidery, called tatreez, was recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage in 2021.
Hisham's Palace near Jericho has one of the largest floor mosaics in the world, including the famous 'Tree of Life'.
The tiny, shimmering Palestine sunbird was adopted as Palestine's national bird in 2015.
Tahitian black pearls, grown in black-lip oysters in lagoons, are French Polynesia's largest export.
The English word 'tattoo' comes from the Polynesian word 'tatau', used in Tahitian, Samoan and Tongan.
Paris 2024's surfing was held at Teahupo'o in Tahiti, 15,000 km from Paris: the farthest an Olympic medal event has been from its host city.
Taputapuātea on Raiatea, once the religious centre of Eastern Polynesia, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017.
The painter Paul Gauguin lived in Tahiti and is buried in Atuona on Hiva Oa in the Marquesas Islands.
Bora Bora, formed by an extinct volcano, is ringed by a lagoon and barrier reef and topped by 727 m Mount Otemanu.
Qatar gets most of its water by desalinating seawater.
At Khor Al Adaid, known as the 'Inland Sea', the sea winds into the desert between dunes up to 67 m high.
Al Zubarah, once a busy pearl-fishing and trading town, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2013.
Qatar banned child camel jockeys in 2005 and ordered that by 2007 all camel races use robot jockeys.
In 2022 Qatar hosted the first FIFA World Cup in the Middle East, and the first played in November and December.
Qatar's North Field is part of by far the world's largest natural gas field, shared with Iran.
Réunion holds the world record for most rain in 24 hours: 1,825 mm at Foc-Foc in January 1966.
Piton de la Fournaise on Réunion is one of Earth's most active volcanoes.
In 1841 Edmond Albius, a 12-year-old enslaved boy on Réunion, invented a quick way to hand-pollinate vanilla flowers.
Réunion's peaks, cirques and cliffs became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010.
The Cirque de Mafate on Réunion can only be reached on foot or by helicopter.
Even though it lies in the Indian Ocean, Réunion uses the euro.
The Danube Delta, mostly in Romania, is Europe's best-preserved delta, with over 320 bird species in summer.
Bucharest's Palace of the Parliament is the heaviest building in the world.
Top Gear's Jeremy Clarkson called Romania's twisting Transfăgărășan mountain road 'the best road in the world'.
Bran Castle is marketed as 'Dracula's Castle', though it's never mentioned in Bram Stoker's novel.
The Merry Cemetery in Săpânța is famous for its brightly painted wooden crosses with funny poems about the dead.
Scărișoara Ice Cave, formed some 3,500 years ago, holds about 75,000 m³ of ice that is up to 20 m thick in places.
Lake Baikal in Siberia is the world's deepest lake (1,642 m) and holds 22–23% of the world's fresh surface water.
Russia spans 11 time zones, from UTC+2 to UTC+12.
The Trans-Siberian Railway runs 9,289 km from Moscow to Vladivostok, making it the longest railway line in the world.
Oymyakon is the coldest permanently inhabited settlement on Earth, once recording −67.7 °C.
The Hermitage in St Petersburg, founded by Catherine the Great in 1764, holds the largest collection of paintings in the world.
The first Russian matryoshka nesting dolls were made in the 1890s.
Rwanda's Volcanoes National Park is one of only three places in the world where you can see wild mountain gorillas.
Rwanda is nicknamed the 'Land of a Thousand Hills' (Pays des mille collines).
Plastic bags have been banned by law in Rwanda since 2008, and any found in luggage are confiscated on arrival.
On Umuganda, the last Saturday of every month, Rwandans do community work like cleaning up their neighbourhoods.
Nyungwe Forest is home to 13 primate species, about a quarter of Africa's total, including chimpanzees.
Lions returned to Rwanda's Akagera National Park in 2015, and black rhinos followed in 2017.

SAH.capitalNote: The status of Western Sahara is disputed. Laayoune, its largest city, lies outside the area shown on this map.

funFacts.text: A conveyor belt about 100 km long, the longest in the world, carries phosphate rock from Bou Craa to the coast.
Dakhla has become a centre for water sports like kitesurfing and windsurfing.
In 1434 Portuguese sailor Gil Eanes sailed past Cape Bojador, a headland so feared that sailors told tales of sea monsters.
Sahrawi tea comes in three glasses: the first bitter like life, the second sweet like love, the third gentle like death.
Sahrawi women traditionally wear the melhfa, a long wrapped cloth that also covers the head.
The Rub' al Khali, or Empty Quarter, is the largest continuous sand desert on Earth.
Saudi Arabia has no permanent rivers, so its water comes from groundwater and desalinated seawater.
Hegra, with over 110 Nabataean tombs carved into sandstone, became Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008.
King Fahd's Fountain in Jeddah shoots seawater up to 312 m high, making it the tallest fountain in the world.
Elephant Rock in AlUla is a 52 m sandstone formation that wind and water shaped like an elephant.
Al-Ahsa Oasis, with more than 2.5 million palm trees, is listed by Guinness as the largest oasis in the world.
Scarborough Shoal is a triangle of reefs and rocks around a lagoon, covering 150 km², with only a few rocks above high tide.
Scarborough Shoal is named after the British ship Scarborough, which ran aground on its rocks in 1748.
Scarborough Shoal's highest point, South Rock, sticks up just 1.8 m above the sea at high tide.

SDN.capitalNote: Government offices have operated temporarily from Port Sudan since 2023.

funFacts.text: About 255 pyramids were built in Nubia, now Sudan: more than double the number built in ancient Egypt.
Sudan's capital Khartoum sits where the Blue Nile and the White Nile meet.
Sudan's Sanganeb coral reef, Dungonab Bay and Mukkawar Island in the Red Sea became a World Heritage Site in 2016.
About 70% of the world's gum arabic, a tree sap used in soft drinks, sweets and medicines, comes from Sudan.
Jebel Barkal, a 104 m flat-topped mesa in Sudan, is surrounded by the ruins of at least 13 ancient temples.
The Western Deffufa at Kerma is an ancient mud-brick temple 18 m tall, with ceremonies held on its top.
South Sudan's white-eared kob, tiang and Mongalla gazelle make one of the largest mammal migrations on Earth, about 1.2 million animals.
The Sudd, a vast swamp formed by the White Nile in South Sudan, is one of the world's largest wetlands.
The shoebill, a stork-like bird with an enormous shoe-shaped bill, has a stronghold in South Sudan's swamps.
Mount Kinyeti in the Imatong Mountains is South Sudan's highest peak, at 3,187 m.
Most Nile lechwe, antelopes that wade and swim, live in South Sudan's Sudd swamps.
Lake Retba near Dakar has pink water from Dunaliella salina algae and was often the finish of the Dakar Rally.
Pointe des Almadies near Dakar is the westernmost point of mainland Africa.
The African Renaissance Monument in Dakar is a 50 m bronze statue, the tallest statue in Africa.
Thieboudienne, rice and fish, is Senegal's national dish and is recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage.
Djoudj National Bird Sanctuary, a UNESCO site, has recorded nearly 3 million birds, with pelicans and flamingos the easiest to spot.
Senegalese wrestling, laamb, is the national sport, and wrestlers recite boasts called bàkk before a match.
Serranilla Bank is a mostly submerged former atoll, with just three small cays and two rocks above the water.
Serranilla Bank is part of the Seaflower Biosphere Reserve, declared by UNESCO in 2000.
Many shipwrecks lie around the shallow reefs of Serranilla Bank.
In 1952 Serranilla Bank saw the last-ever sighting of the now-extinct Caribbean monk seal.
Thanks to land reclamation, Singapore has grown by about 22% since independence in 1965.
Selling chewing gum has been illegal in Singapore since 1992.
The 40 m Rain Vortex inside Jewel Changi Airport is the world's tallest indoor waterfall.
In 2015 Singapore Botanic Gardens became the first tropical botanic garden on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
Singapore's Night Safari, opened in 1994, was the world's first nocturnal zoo.
Singapore's hawker culture of busy food centres was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2020.
The king penguin colony at St Andrews Bay on South Georgia has over 150,000 birds and is probably the largest in the world.
Explorer Ernest Shackleton is buried at Grytviken on South Georgia.
South Georgia's rat eradication was by far the largest ever attempted, and the island has stayed rat-free since.
The wandering albatross, the bird with the longest wingspan (up to 3.7 m), breeds on South Georgia.
Grytviken was a whaling station from 1904 to 1966; the manager's house is now the South Georgia Museum.
Mount Michael in the South Sandwich Islands has a persistent lava lake, a feature known at only eight volcanoes in the world.
Napoleon was exiled to Saint Helena, one of the world's most remote islands, in 1815 and died there in 1821.
Jonathan, a giant tortoise brought to Saint Helena in 1882, is the oldest known living land animal.
Jacob's Ladder in Jamestown is a staircase of 699 steps climbing straight up Ladder Hill.
The Saint Helena plover, called the wirebird for its thin legs, is the national bird and lives nowhere else.
In 1676 astronomer Edmond Halley set up an observatory on Saint Helena and made the first telescopic catalogue of the southern sky.
Saint Helena grows rare green-tipped Bourbon coffee; in 2016 Starbucks sold it for about $145 a pound.
About a quarter of Solomon Islanders carry a gene variant for blond hair that is different from the one behind blond hair in Europeans.
Rennell Island, home to the UNESCO-listed East Rennell, is the largest raised coral atoll in the world.
Malaitan shell money, made in the Langa Langa Lagoon, is the traditional currency of the Solomon Islands.
The prehensile-tailed skink of the Solomon Islands is the world's largest skink and uses its tail as a fifth limb to climb trees.
Marovo Lagoon is the largest double-barrier enclosed lagoon in the world.
On Savo Island, megapode birds bury their eggs in warm sand and let it incubate them.
Portuguese explorer Pedro de Sintra named the coast Serra Leoa, 'lioness mountains', in 1462.
The 968.9-carat Star of Sierra Leone is the fourth-largest gem-quality diamond ever found.
Tiwai Island is home to rare pygmy hippos and 11 species of primates.
Fourah Bay College in Freetown, founded in 1827, was the first Western-style university in West Africa.
Freetown was founded in 1792 as a home for free and freed people, and was christened 'Free Town'.
Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary, founded in 1995, rescues and rehabilitates orphaned chimpanzees in Sierra Leone.
El Salvador is the only country in Central America without a Caribbean coastline.
As the smallest country in continental America, El Salvador is fondly nicknamed 'Pulgarcito de America' (Little Thumb of America).
Joya de Cerén, a Maya village buried by volcanic ash around AD 600, is often called the 'Pompeii of the Americas'.
Pupusas are El Salvador's national dish, and the second Sunday of November is National Pupusa Day.
Izalco volcano erupted almost non-stop from 1770 to 1958, earning it the nickname 'Lighthouse of the Pacific'.
El Salvador's national bird is the torogoz, also called the turquoise-browed motmot.
San Marino claims to have been founded in AD 301, making it the world's oldest surviving sovereign state.
San Marino's Three Towers sit on the three peaks of Monte Titano and appear on both its flag and coat of arms.
San Marino is led by two Captains Regent at the same time, chosen every six months.
San Marino is one of only three countries in the world completely surrounded by another country.
In 1861 San Marino offered US President Abraham Lincoln honorary citizenship, and he gladly accepted.
San Marino's historic centre and Monte Titano became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008.
Somalia's coastline stretches more than 3,333 km, the longest of mainland Africa.
Somalia has the largest population of camels in the world.
Somalia is a major world supplier of fragrant frankincense and myrrh.
The Somali language got the Latin alphabet as its official script only in 1972.
Writer Margaret Laurence called Somalia a 'Nation of Poets' for its rich poetry tradition.
Pasta and lasagne became popular in Somalia during the Italian colonial period, especially in the south.
The Southern Patagonian Ice Field is the world's second-largest continuous ice field outside the polar regions.
The ice field feeds the Perito Moreno Glacier, whose ice dam bursts with a huge flood every year or few years.
The Pío XI Glacier, fed by this ice field, is the largest and longest glacier in the Southern Hemisphere outside Antarctica.
Argentina's Los Glaciares National Park, where many of the ice field's glaciers flow, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981.
Two volcanoes, Lautaro and Viedma, are hidden under the Southern Patagonian Ice Field.
Granite Mount Fitz Roy rises from the ice field; its local name Chaltén means 'smoking mountain' after the clouds around its peak.
Saint Pierre and Miquelon are the only remaining piece of France's old New France empire in North America.
Saint-Pierre lies just 19 km from Newfoundland in Canada.
During US Prohibition, smuggling Canadian whisky through Saint Pierre and Miquelon became a big business.
Miquelon and Langlade are joined by a 10 km sandy strip called the Dune de Langlade.
Although in North America, Saint Pierre and Miquelon has used the euro since 1999.
Every summer Saint Pierre and Miquelon holds a Basque Festival with Basque pelota and other traditional sports.
Île-aux-Marins, a fishing village abandoned in the 1960s, is now a ghost town with a heritage museum in its old school.
Serbia is one of the world's biggest raspberry producers, ranking third in the world in 2023.
Nikola Tesla's ashes are displayed in a gold-plated urn at the Tesla Museum in Belgrade.
The word 'vampire' comes from Serbian 'vampir' and spread in English after news of a Serbian vampire panic in 1725.
The town of Guča hosts a huge annual Balkan brass band festival that started in 1961.
Lepenski Vir on the Danube is a Stone Age settlement famous for fish-like stone sculptures with human faces.
Belgrade sits where the Sava River meets the Danube.
The equator runs right across Ilhéu das Rolas, a tiny islet just off the south of São Tomé island.
São Tomé and Príncipe is Africa's second-smallest country.
Pico Cão Grande is a needle-shaped volcanic spire that shoots up about 370 m above the land around it.
By 1905, São Tomé was the world's largest producer of cocoa.
The whole island of Príncipe has been a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve since 2012.
São Tomé and Príncipe was uninhabited when Portuguese sailors arrived in 1470.
About 90% of Suriname is covered by forest, the highest share of any country in the world.
Suriname is the only independent country outside Europe where Dutch is the official and main language.
Suriname is the smallest country in South America, both by area and population.
The Central Suriname Nature Reserve protects untouched rainforest and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000.
The historic inner city of Paramaribo is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Suriname is one of the few countries where a synagogue stands right next to a mosque.
Slovakia builds more cars per person than any other country in the world.
The huge ruins of Spiš Castle in eastern Slovakia have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1993.
Slovakia's Dobšinská Ice Cave holds about 125,000 m³ of ice and was the first electrically lit cave in Europe.
Bryndzové halušky, potato dumplings with soft sheep's cheese and bacon bits, is one of Slovakia's national dishes.
The mining town of Banská Štiavnica opened the first mining school in the Kingdom of Hungary in 1735.
Vlkolínec is a UNESCO-listed mountain village with the region's most complete group of traditional log houses.
Slovenia's caves are home to the olm, a blind salamander that can live for more than 100 years.
The Lipica stud farm in Slovenia, founded in 1580, is the birthplace of the famous Lipizzaner horses.
About 60% of Slovenia is covered by forest.
Martel's Chamber in Slovenia's Škocjan Caves is the largest known underground chamber in Europe.
In 1936 Sepp Bradl made the first ski jump over 100 m in history at Planica in Slovenia.
World Bee Day on 20 May was Slovenia's idea, adopted by the United Nations in 2017.
Sweden has a whopping 267,570 islands.
Sweden's Icehotel, the world's first ice hotel, is rebuilt every year from blocks of ice cut from the Torne River.
Sweden's 'allemansrätten' lets everyone walk, ski and camp on almost any land, even privately owned.
The modern three-point seat belt was invented by Swedish Volvo engineer Nils Bohlin in 1959.
Swedes love 'fika', a coffee break often enjoyed with pastries like cinnamon buns.
Surströmming, fermented Baltic herring, has one of the most putrid food smells in the world.

SWZ.capitalNote: Mbabane is the administrative capital; Lobamba is the royal and legislative capital.

funFacts.text: Eswatini's Umhlanga, or Reed Dance, brings tens of thousands of young women together each year to cut and present reeds.
Eswatini's Ngwenya Mine is considered the world's oldest mine, worked for red ochre over 41,000 years ago.
Sibebe near Mbabane is the world's largest exposed granite pluton, rising 350 m above the valley.
In 2018 the king changed the country's official name from Swaziland to Eswatini.
Eswatini's flag shows a Nguni shield and two spears, symbols of protection.
Hlane Royal National Park is Eswatini's largest protected area, home to lions, elephants and white rhinos.
At Maho Beach, planes landing at Princess Juliana Airport fly less than 30 m above the sand.
Sint Maarten shares its island with French Saint-Martin, the smallest inhabited island split between two nations.
Guavaberry liqueur, made with rum, is a favourite Christmas drink in Sint Maarten.
The Dutch West India Company came to Sint Maarten to mine salt.
The Dutch built Fort Amsterdam in Sint Maarten in 1631, but Spain captured it within two years.
The Kalinago people called the island Soualiga, meaning 'the island of salt'.
The coco de mer palm, found wild only on two Seychelles islands, has the largest seed in the plant kingdom.
Seychelles' Aldabra Atoll is home to some 180,000 giant tortoises, the largest population in the world.
The Vallée de Mai on Praslin is a UNESCO-listed palm forest where the coco de mer grows wild.
The granite inner islands of Seychelles are fragments of the ancient supercontinent Gondwana.
The rare Seychelles black parrot, the national bird, lives only on the island of Praslin.
Seychelles is made up of 115 islands scattered across the Indian Ocean.
Hama's medieval wooden water wheels, called norias, reach up to 21 m across.
Damascus is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.
Scribes in the ancient Syrian city of Ugarit used the oldest known systematic alphabet, pressed into clay tablets.
Krak des Chevaliers is one of the most important preserved medieval castles in the world and a UNESCO site.
Aleppo soap is made from olive oil and laurel berry oil.
Damask fabric is named after Damascus, a big trading centre on the Silk Road.
The Turks Islands are named after the Turk's cap cactus, whose red top looks like a fez.
The Turks and Caicos rock iguana lives nowhere else in the world.
Salt Cay sits right on the humpback whales' yearly migration route to their breeding grounds.
Making salt from seawater was Salt Cay's main industry for about 300 years, and its ruins still remain.
After orbiting Earth in 1962, astronaut John Glenn splashed down nearby and was brought ashore to Grand Turk.
In ripsaw music, born in Turks and Caicos, a handsaw is played by scraping a knife blade along its teeth.
Chad's Bodélé Depression is the world's largest dust source, and its dust helps fertilise the Amazon rainforest.
Chad is named after Lake Chad, and 'Chad' comes from the Kanuri word for 'lake'.
Chad's Ennedi Massif is a UNESCO-listed sandstone landscape of towers, pillars, bridges and natural arches.
The Lakes of Ounianga are 18 lakes of many colours in the middle of the Sahara, listed by UNESCO in 2012.
Emi Koussi in Chad's Tibesti Mountains is the highest mountain in the Sahara.
The Toumaï skull, a possible early human relative about 7 million years old, was found in Chad's Djurab Desert.
Togo's Koutammakou region is famous for its mud tower houses and is listed by UNESCO.
Togo is less than 115 km wide between Ghana and Benin.
Togo has the fourth-largest phosphate deposits in the world; phosphate is used to make fertiliser.
Mount Agou, at 986 m, is the highest point in Togo.
Fazao-Malfakassa is the largest of Togo's three national parks.
Lake Togo, part of a coastal lagoon, is a popular spot for water sports and pirogue canoe trips.
Bangkok's full ceremonial name is listed by Guinness as the world's longest place name, at 168 letters.
Thailand, then called Siam, was the only country in Southeast Asia never colonised by a European power.
Muay Thai, 'the art of eight limbs', is recognised as Thailand's national sport.
Kitti's hog-nosed bat, or bumblebee bat, from Thailand is the world's smallest bat.
During Songkran, the Thai New Year in April, people celebrate with joyful public water fights.
Lopburi holds a yearly Monkey Buffet Festival, treating its macaques to a feast of fruit and vegetables.
Mountains cover more than 90% of Tajikistan.
Tajikistan's 77 km Fedchenko Glacier is the longest glacier in the world outside the polar regions.
Ismoil Somoni Peak, once called Communism Peak, was the tallest mountain in the whole Soviet Union.
The Usoi Dam, made by a huge landslide in a 1911 earthquake, is the tallest dam in the world, natural or man-made, and holds back Sarez Lake.
Tajikistan's 304 m-tall Nurek Dam was the tallest dam in the world from 1980 until China's Jinping-I Dam overtook it in 2013.
Marco Polo sheep, famous for their long spiralling horns, roam the Pamir Mountains, which reach into Tajikistan.
Iskanderkul, a lake high in Tajikistan's Fann Mountains, takes its name from Alexander the Great.

TKL.capitalNote: Tokelau has no capital; the seat of government rotates yearly among its three atolls.

funFacts.text: In 2012 Tokelau became the world's first 100% solar-powered nation.
Tokelau has no airport, so visitors take a ferry from Samoa that sails for a little over a day.
Tokelau is made up of three tropical coral atolls: Atafu, Nukunonu and Fakaofo.
Tokelau's highest point is just 5 metres above sea level.
Tokelau's '.tk' web domain, once handed out for free, grew into the world's largest country-code domain.
About five times as many people in New Zealand identify as Tokelauan as live in Tokelau itself.
The Darvaza gas crater, nicknamed the 'Door to Hell', has been burning in the Karakum Desert since 1971.
Turkmenistan's Akhal-Teke horses often have a shimmering metallic sheen, and they appear on the national emblem.
In 2013 Ashgabat entered the Guinness records for the world's highest concentration of white marble buildings.
Turkmenistan's flag shows five carpet patterns, called guls, one for each of the country's five major tribes.
The Silk Road city of Merv, now a UNESCO site, may have been the world's largest city in the 12th and 13th centuries.
Turkmenistan has a national holiday for melons: Melon Day, on the second Sunday of August.
Divers have found more reef fish species per site around Atauro Island than anywhere else in the world, up to 315 at one spot.
Timor-Leste's hand-woven tais textiles joined UNESCO's list of heritage in need of urgent safeguarding in 2021.
The 'Timor Hybrid', a natural cross of arabica and robusta coffee born on Timor, was used to breed rust-resistant coffee.
A Timorese legend says a friendly crocodile's body became the island of Timor, which still has a crocodile's shape.
Mount Ramelau, at 2,963 m the highest point in Timor-Leste, lets campers see sunset and sunrise from the same spot.
Timor-Leste adopted the US dollar as its currency in 2000.
Tonga lies just west of the International Date Line and keeps its clocks 13 hours ahead of UTC all year.
Tonga got the nickname 'the Friendly Islands' after the warm welcome Captain Cook received in 1773.
Humpback whales come to Tonga to give birth, and it is one of the few places on Earth where you can swim with them.
The Ha'amonga 'a Maui, a 13th-century stone gateway with 30-40 ton pillars, is nicknamed the 'Stonehenge of the Pacific'.
Tu'i Malila, a radiated tortoise said to have been a gift from Captain Cook to Tonga's royals, lived to about 188.
Trinidad's Pitch Lake is the largest natural deposit of asphalt in the world.
The steelpan, a drum made from oil drums, was developed in Trinidad and Tobago in the 1930s and 1940s and is its national instrument.
Every evening scarlet ibises, Trinidad's national bird, fly back to roost in the mangroves of the Caroni Swamp.
Tobago's Main Ridge Forest Reserve, legally protected since 1776, is one of the oldest protected areas in the world.
In 2012 the Trinidad Moruga Scorpion was named the hottest chilli pepper in the world, at about 1.2 million Scoville units.
Grande Riviere beach in northern Trinidad is regarded as the densest nesting site in the world for giant leatherback turtles.
Star Wars was filmed in Tunisia, and Luke Skywalker's home planet Tatooine is named after the town of Tataouine.
The Roman amphitheatre of El Djem could hold an estimated 35,000 spectators and is one of the best-preserved Roman ruins in the world.
The ruins of ancient Carthage, Rome's great rival, lie about 15 km from Tunis and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Chott el Djerid is the largest salt pan of the Sahara, and in summer it is famous for its mirages.
Harissa, Tunisia's fiery chilli paste, joined UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage list in 2022.
In Matmata, homes were made by digging a big pit in the ground and carving cave rooms around its edge.
Göbekli Tepe in southeastern Turkey, built around 9500 BCE, has the oldest known megaliths in the world.
Cappadocia's Derinkuyu underground city, carved into soft volcanic rock about 85 m deep, could shelter up to 20,000 people.
Istanbul straddles the Bosphorus strait, making it a city on two continents: Europe and Asia.
Pamukkale, meaning 'cotton castle', is a hillside of snow-white limestone terraces fed by 17 hot springs.
The first tulip bulbs reached Vienna from the Ottoman Empire in 1554, kicking off Europe's love of tulips.
Turkish coffee culture and tradition has been on UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage list since 2013.
In 2019 about 8% of Tuvalu's government revenue came from licensing its internet domain, '.tv'.
Tuvalu's highest point is only 4.6 metres above sea level, on the island of Niulakita.
On Funafuti, the airport runway doubles as a space for sports and get-togethers when no planes are using it.
The name Tuvalu means 'eight standing together' in Tuvaluan.
Tuvalu used to be called the Ellice Islands and became its own colony in 1975, then independent in 1978.
Tuvalu's fatele dance-song is repeated louder and quicker as more people join in, until it ends abruptly.
Bubble tea, usually made with chewy tapioca pearls, originated in Taiwan in the 1980s.
Taipei 101 was the tallest building in the world from 2004 until 2010.
Taiwan's highest peak, Yushan (Jade Mountain), at 3,952 m, is 176 m taller than Japan's Mount Fuji.
Portuguese sailors marked Taiwan on their maps in 1542 as 'Ilha Formosa', meaning 'beautiful island'.
Taiwan's garbage trucks play Beethoven's 'Für Elise' so residents know to bring out their rubbish.
Taroko Gorge was carved into marble by the Liwu River, one of only three river gorges in the world cut entirely through pure marble.

TZA.capitalNote: Dodoma is the official capital; some government offices remain in Dar es Salaam.

funFacts.text: Mount Kilimanjaro is Africa's highest mountain and the highest free-standing mountain in the world.
Every year about 1.7 million wildebeest loop through Tanzania's Serengeti in the Great Migration.
The Ngorongoro Crater is the world's largest intact, unfilled volcanic caldera and is home to about 25,000 large animals.
Fossils from Tanzania's Olduvai Gorge have been invaluable for understanding early human evolution.
The blue-violet gem tanzanite is found in only one small area of northern Tanzania.
Queen singer Freddie Mercury was born in Stone Town on the island of Zanzibar.
The town of Jinja sits on Lake Victoria's north shore, right near the source of the River Nile.
Uganda's Bwindi Impenetrable National Park is home to about half of the world's mountain gorillas.
At Murchison Falls the Nile squeezes through a rocky gap only 7 metres wide and tumbles 43 metres.
The Rwenzori Mountains, linked to the legendary 'Mountains of the Moon', have glaciers even though they sit in equatorial Africa.
In the Ishasha area of Queen Elizabeth National Park, lions are famous for climbing trees.
Uganda's flag shows a crested crane, the country's national bird.
Kyiv's Arsenalna station, 105.5 m underground, is the second-deepest metro station in the world.
Near Klevan in Ukraine, trees around a railway line form green arches known as the 'Tunnel of Love'.
Hoverla, in the Carpathian Mountains, is Ukraine's highest peak at 2,061 m.
Ukraine's steppes are known for chernozem, a black soil so fertile it can produce very high harvests.
Petrykivka painting, a Ukrainian folk art of fantastic flowers and birds, has been on UNESCO's intangible heritage list since 2013.
Optymistychna Cave in western Ukraine is the longest gypsum cave in the world, with about 264 km of mapped passages.
Midway Atoll is home to Wisdom, a Laysan albatross first tagged in 1956 and the oldest confirmed wild bird in the world.
About two-thirds of all the world's Laysan albatrosses live on Midway Atoll.
Midway Atoll got its name because it lies roughly halfway between North America and Asia.
Palmyra Atoll is the only incorporated territory of the United States.
Howland Island has a day beacon called Earhart Light, named after Amelia Earhart, who was due to refuel there in 1937.
Wake Island lies west of the International Date Line, so it is almost a day ahead of the 50 US states.
Uruguay hosted the very first FIFA World Cup in 1930, and won it.
Candombe, Uruguay's African-rooted drumming tradition, has been on UNESCO's intangible heritage list since 2009.
Through Plan Ceibal, Uruguay became the first country to give every public primary school pupil their own laptop.
Uruguay's Carnival is considered the longest in the world, with Montevideo's celebrations lasting up to 40 days.
In Punta del Este, a sculpture of five giant fingers pokes out of the sand of Brava beach.

US-DC.capitalNote: It is the city of Washington, the capital of the United States

funFacts.text: Yellowstone, established in 1872, is widely considered the world's first national park.
Death Valley recorded a scorching 56.7 °C (134 °F) on July 10, 1913.
General Sherman, a giant sequoia in California, is the largest known living single-stem tree on Earth by volume.
Kentucky's Mammoth Cave is the longest known cave system in the world, with more than 686 km of mapped passages.
The Statue of Liberty was a gift from the people of France, dedicated in 1886.
The Wright brothers made the first powered airplane flight near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, in 1903.
Uzbekistan is one of only two doubly landlocked countries in the world; the other is Liechtenstein.
Samarkand's Registan square is lined by three grand madrasas covered in intricate mosaic tilework.
Palov (plov), Uzbekistan's beloved rice and meat dish, has been on UNESCO's intangible heritage list since 2016.
Itchan Kala, the walled inner town of Khiva, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1990.
In the 1420s Ulugh Beg built an observatory in Samarkand with part of its giant sextant sunk into a trench in the ground.
Legend says Genghis Khan was so impressed by Bukhara's Kalyan Minaret that he ordered it spared.
The pope has been guarded by the Swiss Guard, in their striped red, blue and yellow Renaissance-style uniforms, since 1506.
Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling in the Vatican between 1508 and 1512.
The Vatican has ATMs with instructions in Latin, possibly the only ones in the world.
White smoke rising from the Sistine Chapel tells the world a new pope has been chosen.
Only 300 metres of the Vatican's railway lies inside the country, making it the shortest national railway in the world.
The Vatican Library, formally founded in 1475, is one of the oldest libraries in the world.
The Pirates of the Caribbean films were shot on Saint Vincent, helping put the country on the tourist map.
The botanical garden in Kingstown, begun in 1765, is one of the oldest in the Western Hemisphere.
William Bligh, of Mutiny on the Bounty fame, brought breadfruit to Saint Vincent's botanical garden around 1793.
The colourful St. Vincent parrot is the national bird and the only kind of parrot on the island.
Green sea turtles feed and nest in the Tobago Cays Marine Park, a favourite spot for snorkelling.
Mustique, a private island in the Grenadines, is popular with celebrities and British royals like Princess Margaret.
Angel Falls in Venezuela is the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall, at 979 metres.
Catatumbo lightning over Lake Maracaibo gives the area the highest lightning density in the world, about 250 strikes per km² a year.
Reports of Mount Roraima, a flat-topped tepui on Venezuela's border, are said to have inspired Conan Doyle's 'The Lost World'.
Arepas, flatbreads made of ground maize dough, are eaten throughout the day in Venezuela.
Venezuela means 'little Venice': Amerigo Vespucci was reminded of Venice by stilt houses on Lake Maracaibo.
The Orinoco crocodile, the largest predator in the Americas, lives only in the Orinoco river basin of Venezuela and Colombia.
The Baths on Virgin Gorda is a beach of giant granite boulders forming tidal pools, tunnels and grottoes.
Unlike the other British Virgin Islands, Anegada is a flat coral island rather than a volcanic one.
Norman Island is one of the islands said to have inspired Robert Louis Stevenson's 'Treasure Island'.
Although it is a British territory, the British Virgin Islands has used the US dollar since 1959.
The Painkiller rum cocktail was created in the 1970s at the Soggy Dollar Bar on Jost Van Dyke.
The critically endangered Anegada ground iguana survives only on Anegada and nearby Guana Island.
The US Virgin Islands is the only part of the United States where people drive on the left.
In 1917 the United States bought the islands from Denmark for $25 million in gold coin.
Virgin Islands National Park covers almost 60% of the island of St. John.
At Buck Island Reef off St. Croix, snorkellers can follow a marked underwater trail through the reef.
Point Udall on St. Croix is the easternmost point of the United States.
Founding father Alexander Hamilton spent part of his childhood on St. Croix, where his mother ran a small shop.
Son Doong in Vietnam is the world's largest natural cave, and sunlight through holes in its roof lets a jungle grow inside.
Ha Long Bay is dotted with 1,969 islets, most of them limestone, rising straight out of the sea.
Water puppetry dates back to the 11th century in northern Vietnam, where the first shows were held right in a rice paddy.
The famous noodle soup phở comes from northern Vietnam, where it appeared in the early 20th century.
The saola, a rare forest animal with long pointed horns, was discovered by scientists in Vietnam in 1992.
Vietnam is the world's second-biggest coffee producer after Brazil, and 97% of its coffee is robusta.
On Pentecost Island men leap from tall towers with vines tied to their ankles, a ritual that gave Oxford students the idea for bungee jumping.
Vanuatu has the most languages per person of any country, with over 100 local languages for fewer than 300,000 people.
Mount Yasur on Tanna has been erupting almost non-stop for centuries, and its glow drew Captain Cook to the island in 1774.
Hideaway Island in Vanuatu opened the world's first underwater post office in 2003.
Vanuatu sand drawing, traced with one finger in a continuous line, is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.
Vanuatu's flag shows a curled boar's tusk, a symbol of tradition and prosperity.
Wallis and Futuna still has three traditional kings, who sit on the Territorial Council.
Wallis Island is named after British explorer Samuel Wallis, who sailed past it in 1767.
Futuna and Alofi are the Hoorn Islands, named by Dutch explorers in 1616 after the Dutch city of Hoorn.
Lake Lalolalo on Wallis is a volcanic crater lake that is almost a perfect circle.
Talietumu on Wallis is a Tongan fort built around 1450, when the Tongan empire was expanding.
Wallis and Futuna uses the CFP franc as its currency rather than the euro.

WSB.capitalNote: Episkopi Cantonment is the administrative seat for both Akrotiri and Dhekelia.

funFacts.text: Between 2,000 and 20,000 greater flamingos spend the winter on Akrotiri Salt Lake.
Cape Gata on the Akrotiri peninsula is the southernmost point of the island of Cyprus.
Akrotiri's wetlands were listed under the Ramsar Convention as a wetland of international importance in 2003.
Akrotiri uses the euro, making it the only place under British rule with the euro as official currency.
The Aetokremnos rock shelter on the Akrotiri peninsula holds the earliest undisputed signs of humans on Cyprus, alongside pygmy hippo bones.
Legend says hundreds of cats were brought to the Monastery of St Nicholas of the Cats at Akrotiri to fight off snakes.
In 2011 Samoa skipped Friday 30 December entirely when it jumped to the other side of the International Date Line.
In 2009 Samoa switched from driving on the right to driving on the left.
Author Robert Louis Stevenson spent his last years in Samoa, where he took the name Tusitala, 'teller of tales'.
Samoa's traditional male tattoo, the pe'a, covers the body from the waist down to the knees.
To Sua Ocean Trench on Upolu is a natural swimming hole that you climb down into on a ladder.
At the Alofaaga Blowholes on Savai'i, waves force seawater up through lava tubes, making fountains every few seconds.

YEM.capitalNote: Sanaa is the constitutional capital; the internationally recognised government is based in Aden.

funFacts.text: Yemen's Socotra island has the umbrella-shaped dragon's blood tree, and over a third of its plants grow nowhere else.
Shibam's mudbrick tower houses earned it the nickname 'Manhattan of the Desert' and made it a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Mocha coffee is named after the Yemeni port of Mocha, once a major marketplace for coffee.
Old houses in Sana'a look like ancient skyscrapers, up to 8 storeys high and decorated with geometric patterns.
Dar al-Hajar, the 'Rock Palace' near Sana'a, has seven floors built to follow the natural shape of the rock beneath it.

ZAF.capitalNote: South Africa has three capitals: Pretoria (executive), Cape Town (legislative) and Bloemfontein (judicial).

funFacts.text: South Africa has 12 official languages, after South African Sign Language became official in 2023.
The world's first human heart transplant was performed in Cape Town in 1967 by Dr Christiaan Barnard.
The Cape Floral Kingdom, the smallest of the world's six floral kingdoms, lies entirely within South Africa.
Sterkfontein in the Cradle of Humankind near Johannesburg yielded over a third of all early hominid fossils found before 2010.
Rooibos tea comes from a plant found wild only in a small part of South Africa's Western Cape.
Tugela Falls in the Drakensberg drops 948 m, and some measurements rank it as the tallest waterfall in the world.
Close to ten million straw-coloured fruit bats gather in Kasanka National Park each year, said to be the world's largest mammal migration.
At Devil's Pool on the Zambian side of Victoria Falls, swimmers can splash right at the lip of the falls in the dry season.
South Luangwa National Park is known as the birthplace of the walking safari.
In the Kuomboka ceremony, the Lozi king sails on his royal barge from the flooding Zambezi plains to higher ground.
The Kabwe skull, also called Broken Hill Man, is a 300,000-year-old human fossil found in Zambia in 1921.
The rare, giant-billed shoebill stork is the most notable bird of Zambia's Bangweulu Swamps.
The stone walls of Great Zimbabwe, which gave the country its name, were built without mortar from the 11th century onward.
Victoria Falls, shared with Zambia, is called Mosi-oa-Tunya, 'the smoke that thunders', and is the largest sheet of falling water on Earth.
Lake Kariba, shared with Zambia, is the world's largest man-made lake by volume.
The Matobo Hills have balancing granite boulders and over 3,000 registered rock art sites.
The bird on Zimbabwe's flag is based on soapstone bird carvings found at Great Zimbabwe.
The Chinhoyi Caves hold the Sleeping Pool, a pool of cobalt-blue water where divers can see 50 metres or more.
